knoblauch.etymology_derivation: Old High German chlobalouh, literally clove leek; Knob- comes from klieben, meaning to cleave, and Lauch is cognate with English leek, which garlic preserves in its own spear-leek compound. [wiktionary]

mehl.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic melu; English meal, in its older sense of ground grain, is a direct cognate. [wiktionary]

nudel.context_translation: The noodles cook for ten minutes.
nudel.etymology_derivation: Attested since the 16th century with unknown deeper origin, possibly a variant of Knödel; English noodle was borrowed from German Nudel. [wiktionary]

öl.context_phrase: Ich brate das Ei in Öl.
öl.context_translation: I fry the egg in oil.
öl.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic oli, meaning olive oil, ultimately from Latin oleum; English oil descends from the same early Latin loan into Old English. [wiktionary]

senf.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic senap, an early borrowing of Latin sinapis, itself from Greek; English keeps the same word only in technical sinap terms and uses mustard instead. [wiktionary]

mineralwasser.context_translation: I am drinking a cold mineral water.
mineralwasser.etymology_derivation: Compound of Mineral and Wasser; Mineral matches English mineral, a Latin loan, and Wasser corresponds to English water via the t to ss shift. [wiktionary]

mittagessen.context_phrase: Das Mittagessen ist um zwölf Uhr.
mittagessen.etymology_derivation: Compound of Mittag and Essen; Mittag is literally mid day with the d to t correspondence, and essen corresponds to English eat via the t to ss shift. [wiktionary]

geschmack.context_phrase: Der Kuchen hat einen guten Geschmack.
geschmack.context_translation: The cake has a good taste.
geschmack.etymology_derivation: From Old High German gismac, from West Germanic smakku; English smack and smatch are cognates of the same taste root, and the ge prefix has no English counterpart. [wiktionary]

pizza.context_phrase: Wir bestellen eine Pizza mit Käse.
pizza.context_translation: We are ordering a pizza with cheese.
pizza.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian pizza, ultimately from Neapolitan via Medieval Greek; English pizza is the same borrowing. [wiktionary]

müsli.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Alemannic Muesli, a diminutive of Mus, meaning porridge; Mus is cognate with English mush, and English borrowed the word muesli from German. [wiktionary]

olive.context_phrase: Die Pizza mit Oliven schmeckt gut.
olive.context_translation: The pizza with olives tastes good.
olive.etymology_derivation: From Latin oliva, partly through Middle High German olive; English olive is the same Latin loan. [wiktionary]

waffel.context_phrase: Ich esse die Waffel mit Marmelade.
waffel.context_translation: I eat the waffle with jam.
waffel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Middle Dutch wafel; English waffle and wafer come from the same Dutch and Germanic word. [wiktionary]

huhn.context_phrase: Das Huhn legt jeden Tag ein Ei.
huhn.context_translation: The chicken lays an egg every day.
huhn.etymology_derivation: Huhn — from Middle High German huon and Proto-West Germanic *hōn, kin to Dutch hoen and English hen; all from the same Germanic fowl family (PIE *keh₂n-). [wiktionary]

hähnchen.context_phrase: Wir essen Hähnchen mit Reis und Salat.
hähnchen.context_translation: We are eating chicken with rice and salad.
hähnchen.etymology_derivation: Hähnchen — diminutive of Hahn (rooster) with the -chen suffix; Hahn is the old Germanic cock-word, the same family as English hen (PIE *keh₂n-). [wiktionary]

schweinefleisch.etymology_derivation: Schweinefleisch — a compound of Schwein (pig) and Fleisch (flesh, meat); Wiktionary compares the exact English calque swineflesh, so swine and flesh are both true cognates here. [wiktionary]

rindfleisch.context_phrase: Ich kaufe Rindfleisch für die Suppe.
rindfleisch.context_translation: I am buying beef for the soup.
rindfleisch.etymology_derivation: Rindfleisch — a compound of Rind (cow, from Proto-Germanic *hrinþaz, ultimately PIE *ḱerh₂- head) and Fleisch (flesh); English lost Rind and took French beef instead. [wiktionary]

lamm.context_translation: We are grilling lamb on Sunday.
lamm.etymology_derivation: Lamm — from Proto-Germanic *lambaz, the exact cognate of English lamb; the silent b is a shared West Germanic quirk. [wiktionary]

schinken.context_phrase: Ich möchte Schinken und Käse, bitte.
schinken.context_translation: I would like ham and cheese, please.
schinken.etymology_derivation: Schinken — originally a shank or thigh, from Proto-Germanic *skinkō; cognate with English shank and dialectal skink, a shin of beef. [wiktionary]

soße.etymology_derivation: Soße — borrowed from French sauce, from Latin salsa (salted), so both English sauce and German Soße carry the same Latin salt-word. [wiktionary]

joghurt.context_phrase: Zum Frühstück esse ich Joghurt mit Obst.
joghurt.context_translation: For breakfast I eat yogurt with fruit.
joghurt.etymology_derivation: Joghurt — borrowed from Ottoman Turkish yoğurt, exactly like English yogurt; standard German uses der, Austria and Switzerland often das. [wiktionary]

kakao.etymology_derivation: Kakao — borrowed from Spanish cacao, from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl (cacao bean); English cocoa and cacao share the same Nahuatl source. [wiktionary]

limonade.context_phrase: Im Sommer trinke ich gern Limonade.
limonade.context_translation: In summer I like to drink lemonade.
limonade.etymology_derivation: Limonade — borrowed from French limonade, the same drink-word English took as lemonade; the lemon itself traveled from Asia through Persian and Arabic. [wiktionary]

schokolade.context_phrase: Die Schokolade ist für die Kinder.
schokolade.context_translation: The chocolate is for the children.
schokolade.etymology_derivation: Schokolade — borrowed via Dutch chocolade from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl; English chocolate comes from the same Spanish word. [wiktionary]

keks.context_phrase: Ich nehme einen Keks zum Kaffee.
keks.context_translation: I am taking a cookie with my coffee.
keks.etymology_derivation: Keks — a 1900s borrowing of English cakes, popularized when Bahlsen renamed Leibniz-Cakes to Leibniz-Keks in 1911; northern German uses der, the south often das. [wiktionary]

torte.context_phrase: Zum Geburtstag backen wir eine Torte.
torte.context_translation: We are baking a cake for the birthday.
torte.etymology_derivation: Torte — 15th century, from Middle French tarte and tourte, later reinforced by Italian torta, from Late Latin torta (round loaf); English torte was borrowed back from German. [wiktionary]

brötchen.context_phrase: Ich kaufe jeden Morgen frische Brötchen.
brötchen.context_translation: I buy fresh rolls every morning.
brötchen.etymology_derivation: Brötchen — diminutive of Brot (bread), which is cognate with English bread; both trace to PIE *bʰrewh₁-, the root of brew. [wiktionary]

toast.etymology_derivation: Toast — borrowed straight from English toast, with toasten and Toaster as later German offshoots. [wiktionary]

marmelade.etymology_derivation: Marmelade — 16th century, from Middle French marmelade, from Portuguese marmelada (quince jam); English marmalade took the same route. [wiktionary]

mahlzeit.context_phrase: Wir essen drei Mahlzeiten am Tag.
mahlzeit.context_translation: We eat three meals a day.
mahlzeit.etymology_derivation: Mahlzeit — Mahl (meal) plus Zeit (time); Wiktionary compares English mealtide, so Mahl is a direct cognate of meal and Zeit of tide, whose t became z in German. [wiktionary]

getränk.etymology_derivation: Getränk — a collective built on the old word Trank (drink), the same root as trinken; English drink shows the old d where German shifted it to t. [wiktionary]

süß.context_phrase: Der Kuchen ist zu süß für mich.
süß.context_translation: The cake is too sweet for me.
süß.etymology_derivation: süß — from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, PIE *swéh₂dus, exactly cognate with English sweet; the final t shifted to ß and the old w was lost before the rounded vowel. [wiktionary]

sauer.etymology_derivation: sauer — from Proto-Germanic *sūraz, PIE *súHros, the exact cognate of English sour; the long ū diphthongized to au in both languages. [wiktionary]

bitter.context_phrase: Der Kaffee ohne Zucker ist bitter.
bitter.etymology_derivation: bitter — from Proto-Germanic *bitraz, the very same Germanic word as English bitter; German sources tie it to beißen (to bite), the biting taste. [wiktionary]

salzig.etymology_derivation: salzig — from Salz (salt) plus -ig; the old t survives in English salt but shifted to z in German Salz, the Sibilant Shift at work. [wiktionary]

lebensmittel.context_translation: We buy groceries at the supermarket.
lebensmittel.etymology_derivation: Lebensmittel — Leben (life, cognate with live, whose v German closed to b) plus Mittel (means, cognate with middle via the d to t stop shift); literally means of life. [wiktionary]

appetit.context_phrase: Ich habe großen Appetit auf Kuchen.
appetit.context_translation: I have a big appetite for cake.
appetit.etymology_derivation: Appetit — borrowed via Old French from Late Latin appetītus (striving, desire); English appetite is the very same Latin word. [wiktionary]

gewürz.context_phrase: Diese Suppe braucht noch ein Gewürz.
gewürz.context_translation: This soup needs one more spice.
gewürz.etymology_derivation: Gewürz — a 14th-century collective of Wurz (wort, herb, root), compared by Wiktionary with English wort; spices are literally the old herbs. [wiktionary]

menü.context_phrase: Ich bestelle das Menü mit Suppe.
menü.context_translation: I am ordering the set menu with soup.
menü.etymology_derivation: Menü — borrowed from French menu, the same word behind English menu; its computing sense later came in as a semantic loan from English. [wiktionary]

farbe.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *farwō 'color' (Old High German farawa), from the PIE root *perḱ- 'colored'; no English cognate is listed on the page. [wiktionary]

violett.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French violet, the flower name — the page's own derivation; English uses the identical word for the identical flower and color. [wiktionary]

golden.etymology_derivation: Gold 'gold' + the suffix -en 'made of' — the page explicitly lists English golden as a cognate (Proto-Germanic *gulþīnaz). [wiktionary]

jahreszeit.context_phrase: Es gibt vier Jahreszeiten im Jahr.
jahreszeit.context_translation: There are four seasons in a year.
jahreszeit.etymology_derivation: Jahr + Zeit — year-time; Jahr is the twin of English year and Zeit the twin of tide, which originally meant time. [wiktionary]

zahl.context_phrase: Die Zahl sieben ist meine Glückszahl.
zahl.context_translation: The number seven is my lucky number.
zahl.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *talō — the entry lists English tale as a cognate, the same tal-root as tell; the initial t became z. [wiktionary]

nummer.etymology_derivation: From Italian numero, from Latin numerus — the same Latin word that gives English number. [wiktionary]

hälfte.context_phrase: Ich esse nur die Hälfte des Kuchens.
hälfte.context_translation: I eat only half of the cake.
hälfte.etymology_derivation: halb + the deadjectival suffix -te — the twin of half; the entry notes the old b ↔ ft alternation was never levelled. [wiktionary]

erst.context_phrase: Der Zug fährt erst um zehn.
erst.context_translation: The train does not leave until ten.
erst.etymology_derivation: The twin of archaic English erst, as in erstwhile — the English entry lists German erste as a cognate of the same Germanic superlative. [wiktionary]

letzte.context_phrase: Der letzte Bus fährt um elf.
letzte.context_translation: The last bus leaves at eleven.
letzte.etymology_derivation: Historically the superlative of lat — the twin of late; the entry lists English latest and last as cognates. [wiktionary]

nächste.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Hamburg.
nächste.context_translation: Next week I am going to Hamburg.
nächste.etymology_derivation: The superlative of nah — the twin of next, which was originally nighest, the superlative of nigh. [wiktionary]

doppelt.etymology_derivation: Past participle of doppeln, borrowed from Old French doble — the very word that became English double. [wiktionary]

zählen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *taljaną, the causative of the tal-root — the same family as English tell and tale; the initial t became z, as in two, zwei. [wiktionary]

rechnen.etymology_derivation: The twin of English reckon — the entry lists English reckon as its English cognate, both from the PIE root *h₃reǵ-. [wiktionary]

rechnung.etymology_derivation: rechnen + -ung — the twin of English reckoning; the entry lists English reckoning as a cognate. [wiktionary]

menge.context_translation: A lot of people were there.
menge.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *managį̄ — the twin of English many, which kept the older vowel. [wiktionary]

neu.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German niuwe, Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, the exact twin of English new; both go back to the same Indo-European root. [wiktionary]

schnell.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German snel, Proto-Germanic *snellaz, meaning quick and bold; the exact English cognate is the rare word snell, still heard in northern England and Scotland. [wiktionary]

langsam.etymology_derivation: Built exactly like English longsome: lang (long) + the suffix -sam, from Proto-West Germanic *langasam. English lost longsome, but the pieces and the pattern are identical. [wiktionary]

stark.etymology_derivation: From Old High German stark, Proto-West Germanic *stark; the everyday English word stark, as in stark naked, is the very same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

schwach.context_phrase: Nach der Krankheit war er schwach.
schwach.context_translation: After the illness he was weak.
schwach.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German swach, Proto-West Germanic *swak; the English cousins are the dialectal word swack, meaning nimble or lively, and Scots swack. [wiktionary]

hart.context_phrase: Das Brot ist heute sehr hart.
hart.context_translation: The bread is very hard today.
hart.etymology_derivation: From Old High German hart, Proto-Germanic *harduz, the exact twin of English hard; both trace to the same Indo-European root meaning strong. [wiktionary]

fremd.context_translation: The city was strange to me.
fremd.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fremidi, Proto-West Germanic *framiþī; English once had the identical word fremd, meaning foreign or strange, now obsolete, and Dutch keeps vreemd. [wiktionary]

eigen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *aiganaz, the past participle of the verb meaning to have or own; it is the exact parallel of English own, which descends from the same participle of the same verb. [wiktionary]

ernst.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ernust, Proto-Germanic *ernustuz; the English cognate is earnest, as in an earnest promise. [wiktionary]

wichtig.context_phrase: Wasser ist wichtig für die Gesundheit.
wichtig.etymology_derivation: From the root of Gewicht (weight) plus -ig; the entry itself compares English weighty, which builds importance out of weight with the very same metaphor. [wiktionary]

interessant.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French interessant; it belongs with Interesse and interessieren, and English interesting grew from the same Latin source, so the two are partners rather than twins. [wiktionary]

lustig.etymology_derivation: Lust (desire, joy) plus -ig; Lust is the exact cognate of English lust, from Proto-Germanic *lustuz, though in German the sexual shade is weak and the word still means plain pleasure, as in Lust haben. [wiktionary]

dumm.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German tump, Old High German tumb, Proto-Germanic *dumbaz, the exact twin of English dumb; German smoothed the -mb- cluster to -mm- and kept the old meaning. [wiktionary]

klug.context_phrase: Das Mädchen ist klug und freundlich.
klug.context_translation: The girl is clever and friendly.
klug.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German klok via the Lower Rhineland, Proto-Germanic *klokaz; cognates include Old Norse klokr and dialectal Dutch kloek. Standard English has no cousin of this word. [wiktionary]

freundlich.etymology_derivation: Freund (friend) plus -lich; the whole compound is documented back to Proto-Germanic *frijondlikaz, matching English friendly part for part, and the -lich suffix is the same element as English -ly. [wiktionary]

höflich.etymology_derivation: Hof (court, farm) plus -lich, literally courtly, in the manner of the court; the entry parallels it with Old French cortois, which gave English courteous — polite speech learned at court in both languages. [wiktionary]

ehrlich.etymology_derivation: Ehre (honour) plus -lich, inherited from Middle High German erlich and Old High German erlih, built on the old honour root of Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys-. [wiktionary]

schmutzig.etymology_derivation: Schmutz (dirt) plus -ig; the entry says to compare English smutty, a word from the same Germanic family of dirty words with the same -y ending. [wiktionary]

geschlossen.context_phrase: Das Geschäft ist am Sonntag geschlossen.
geschlossen.context_translation: The shop is closed on Sunday.
geschlossen.etymology_derivation: Past participle of schließen (to close), from Proto-Germanic *slūtaną, to lock or shut; cognate with Dutch sluiten and English slot, which first meant the bolt or bar of a door. [wiktionary]

fertig.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fartig, literally journey-ready, from fart (journey), the ancestor of modern Fahrt; the root belongs with the Germanic travel word behind English fare, and Dutch has the parallel vaardig. [wiktionary]

sicher.etymology_derivation: Borrowed very early, already in Old High German, from Latin securus (free from care); that is the same Latin word that later reached English as secure and sure. [wiktionary]

gefährlich.etymology_derivation: Gefahr (danger) plus -lich; Gefahr goes back to Proto-Germanic *fērō, which is also the ancestor of English fear — German kept the old meaning danger, while English drifted to the feeling that danger produces. [wiktionary]

frei.etymology_derivation: From Old High German frī, Proto-West Germanic *frī, the exact twin of English free; both go back to the Indo-European root meaning beloved, the same root that gave German Freund and English friend. [wiktionary]

still.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German stille, Proto-West Germanic *stillī; English still is the same word, and both kept the sense of motionless and silent. [wiktionary]

satt.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sat, Proto-Germanic *sadaz, meaning sated or full; the exact cognate is English sad, which originally meant sated before it drifted to its modern sorrowful sense. [wiktionary]

gleich.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, having the same form, built from ga- plus the ancestor of -like; the English twin is alike, and the suffix inside it is the same element as English -like and -ly. [wiktionary]

mutig.etymology_derivation: Mut (courage) plus -ig, Proto-Germanic *mōdagaz, whose English twin is moody — in Old English moody still meant brave and only later slid to gloomy. [wiktionary]

lecker.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German lecker, tied to the verb lecken, to lick, Proto-West Germanic *likkōn; the entry points to English lick as the relative, so the word family is literally about licking. [wiktionary]

einfach.etymology_derivation: ein 'one' plus the suffix -fach '-fold': literally onefold, the exact comparison Wiktionary itself draws with English onefold. [wiktionary]

schwierig.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German swiric 'full of boils', built on Schwäre 'ulcer'; Wiktionary warns it is often connected to schwer but is unrelated. [wiktionary]

weniger.etymology_derivation: Comparative of wenig, built on the Proto-Germanic root *wainagaz that Wiktionary ties to English woe: from woe-like, miserable to few and less. [wiktionary]

ruhig.etymology_derivation: From Ruhe 'rest, calm' + -ig; Middle High German ruowec meant quiet. [wiktionary]

ängstlich.etymology_derivation: From Angst 'fear, dread' + the suffix -lich — literally angst-like, inclined to fear. [wiktionary]

neugierig.etymology_derivation: A Middle Low German formation of neu 'new' + gierig 'greedy' — greedy for the new; Dutch nieuwsgierig and Norwegian nysgjerrig are built the same way. [wiktionary]

toll.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *dulaz 'foolish, dazed' — the same word as English dull, which etymonline lists beside German toll; German hardened d to t and the sense flipped from mad to great. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

wunderbar.etymology_derivation: Wunder 'wonder' + -bar '-able' — literally wonder-able; Wunder is the twin of English wonder (Proto-Germanic *wundran, per etymonline). [wiktionary] [etymonline]

schrecklich.etymology_derivation: From Schreck 'fright, shock' + the suffix -lich, first attested in Late Middle High German — literally frightful. [wiktionary]

schlimm.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *slimbaz 'crooked, oblique' — the page lists English slim as a cognate; schlimm slid from crooked to bad, and Middle Dutch slim also meant bad. [wiktionary]

fröhlich.etymology_derivation: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *frawalīkaz: froh 'cheerful' + the suffix -lich. [wiktionary]

viel.context_translation: We are having a lot of fun.
viel.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *felu 'many', from PIE *pleh₁- — English once had the twin word fele 'many', the very entry Wiktionary points to. [wiktionary]

wenig.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wainagaz 'miserable', its vowel blended with Old High German wē, akin to English woe: the woe-word came to mean little, few. [wiktionary]

ordentlich.etymology_derivation: From ordnen 'to put in order' + -lich; Ordnung 'order' is the same family. [wiktionary]

breit.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braidaz — the exact twin of English broad (Old English brād), with German breit named as its cognate by etymonline. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

schmal.context_phrase: Der Weg ist schmal und steil.
schmal.context_translation: The path is narrow and steep.
schmal.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *smalaz 'narrow, small' — the page lists English small as the direct cognate; German kept the narrow sense. [wiktionary]

wild.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wilþijaz — the exact twin of English wild; the English entry on the same page names German wild as its cognate. [wiktionary]

sanft.context_phrase: Die Musik ist sanft und leise.
sanft.context_translation: The music is gentle and quiet.
sanft.etymology_derivation: West Germanic *samft(ī) — the page lists soft as the only English cognate; the root may reach back to *sem- 'one'. [wiktionary]

faul.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fūlaz 'rotten, putrid' — the twin of English foul, which the page lists as a cognate; German diphthongized the vowel, and the sense slid from rotten to lazy, idleness as moral rot. [wiktionary]

seltsam.etymology_derivation: Middle High German seltsām, built with the suffix -sam, which the page glosses as English -some; English seldom is listed as a cognate, German having hardened d to t in the root seld-. [wiktionary]

möglich.etymology_derivation: From mögen 'to be able' + -lich: literally may-ly, what may happen — mögen goes back to the same PIE root *megʰ- that produced English may. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

norden.context_translation: In the north it often rains.
norden.etymology_derivation: The compass noun from Nord, the twin of north; used with im for in the north. [wiktionary]

süden.context_phrase: Im Süden ist die Sonne stärker.
süden.context_translation: In the south the sun is stronger.
süden.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German süden, ultimately Proto-Germanic *sunþanē — the old noun *sunþrą gave both English south and German Süd (th → d). [wiktionary]

osten.context_phrase: Der Wind kommt aus dem Osten.
osten.context_translation: The wind comes from the east.
osten.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ostan, from Proto-Germanic *austrą — the same root as English east, ultimately from the dawn root *ausos, as in Latin aurora. [wiktionary]

westen.context_phrase: Die Sonne geht im Westen unter.
westen.context_translation: The sun sets in the west.
westen.etymology_derivation: The compass noun from West, the twin of west; used with im for in the west. [wiktionary]

hinten.context_translation: The toilet is at the back on the left.
hinten.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hindanē — the same hind root as English behind and hind; German shifted d to t (the entry points to hinter for the consonantism). [wiktionary]

drüben.context_translation: The post office is over there.
drüben.etymology_derivation: From a rare üben, a variant of über formed by the analogy of unter/unten and ober/oben — literally over yonder; über is the twin of over. [wiktionary]

gegenüber.context_phrase: Der Supermarkt ist gegenüber der Bank.
gegenüber.context_translation: The supermarket is opposite the bank.
gegenüber.etymology_derivation: gegen + über — literally over-against; über is the twin of English over (both from PIE *upér) and gegen the twin of against. [wiktionary]

entlang.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Middle Low German entlanc, essentially in lang — the lang element is the twin of English long, so it works just like along. [wiktionary]

gegen.context_phrase: Das Spiel beginnt gegen drei Uhr.
gegen.context_translation: The game starts at about three o'clock.
gegen.etymology_derivation: The twin of English against — both from Proto-Germanic *gagin; the entry lists against as a cognate. [wiktionary]

person.context_translation: I do not know this person.
person.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German persōn, the same Latin loan as English person. [wiktionary]

leute.context_translation: Many people are waiting at the station.
leute.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *liudiz, kin to the Old English leode (men, people); German keeps the plural-only collective with the standard article die Leute. [wiktionary]

gast.context_phrase: Wir haben heute Gäste zum Essen.
gast.context_translation: We have guests for dinner today.
gast.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *gastiz, the exact twin of English guest; Latin hostis, enemy, shows the older guest-host pair. [wiktionary]

feind.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fijandz, the hating one, the exact twin of English fiend; both are the participle of the same hate verb. [wiktionary]

kollege.context_phrase: Mein Kollege kommt morgen ins Büro.
kollege.context_translation: My colleague is coming to the office tomorrow.
kollege.etymology_derivation: From Latin collega, the same loan that gives English colleague. [wiktionary]

held.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *haliþ, hero, cognate with Old English hæleþ, a relative of the English health and hale family; the final th hardened to d. [wiktionary]

möbel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed in the 15th century from Middle French meuble, from Latin mobilis, meaning movable; English mobile comes from the same Latin adjective. [wiktionary]

wohnzimmer.context_translation: We are sitting in the living room.
wohnzimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of wohnen and Zimmer; Zimmer corresponds to English timber via the t to z shift. [wiktionary]

schlafzimmer.context_translation: The child sleeps in the bedroom.
schlafzimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of Schlaf and Zimmer; schlafen corresponds to English sleep, with the medial p appearing as f in German. [wiktionary]

badezimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of baden and Zimmer; Bad corresponds to English bath via the th to d shift. [wiktionary]

kinderzimmer.context_translation: The child plays in the children's room.
kinderzimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of Kind and Zimmer with linking er; Kind is cognate with English kin, and Zimmer with English timber. [wiktionary]

esszimmer.context_translation: The meal is in the dining room.
esszimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of essen and Zimmer; essen corresponds to English eat via the t to ss shift. [wiktionary]

flur.context_translation: The shoes are standing in the hallway.
flur.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic floraz; English floor is a direct cognate that kept the old sense, while German Flur narrowed to mean hallway. [wiktionary]

keller.context_translation: The bicycles are standing in the basement.
keller.etymology_derivation: From Old High German kellari, from West Germanic kellari, an early loan of Late Latin cellarium; English cellar is the same Latin word through Old French. [wiktionary]

dachboden.context_phrase: Der Koffer ist auf dem Dachboden.
dachboden.context_translation: The suitcase is in the attic.
dachboden.etymology_derivation: Compound of Dach and Boden, literally roof floor; Dach corresponds to English thatch via the th to d shift, and Boden to English bottom via the d to t shift. [wiktionary]

etage.context_phrase: Wir wohnen in der dritten Etage.
etage.context_translation: We live on the third floor.
etage.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French étage; English stage is a doublet from the same Old French word estage. [wiktionary]

treppe.context_phrase: Die Kinder laufen die Treppe hoch.
treppe.context_translation: The children run up the stairs.
treppe.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic trappa, from the PIE root dreb, meaning to tread or trample; the same stepping root underlies English tread and trip. [wiktionary]

aufzug.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German ufzuc, a verbal noun of aufziehen, meaning to draw or lift up; the Zug element belongs to the ziehen root cognate with English tow, the t appearing as z in German. [wiktionary]

haustür.context_phrase: Der Schlüssel steckt in der Haustür.
haustür.context_translation: The key is in the front door.
haustür.etymology_derivation: Compound of Haus and Tür; Tür corresponds to English door via the d to t shift, the textbook pair of the dental shift. [wiktionary]

kissen.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic kussin, an early borrowing of Latin culcita, meaning bolster or quilted cushion; English quilt is a later French loan of the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

handtuch.context_translation: The towel is hanging in the bath.
handtuch.etymology_derivation: Attested as Old High German hanttuoh; a compound of Hand and Tuch, literally hand cloth, with Hand a direct cognate of English hand. [wiktionary]

seife.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic saipo, from the PIE root seyb, meaning to pour or trickle; English soap is a direct cognate, its p corresponding to German f after the High German shift. [wiktionary]

kamm.context_phrase: Ich brauche einen Kamm für die Haare.
kamm.context_translation: I need a comb for my hair.
kamm.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic kambaz, from PIE gombhos, meaning tooth; English comb is a direct cognate, and both keep the old idea that a comb is full of teeth. [wiktionary]

klingel.context_phrase: Die Klingel läutet an der Tür.
klingel.context_translation: The doorbell is ringing at the door.
klingel.etymology_derivation: From the verb klingen, meaning to ring or sound; the same Germanic kling root underlies English clink. [wiktionary]

schloss.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sloz, ablaut to the verb schließen, meaning to close or lock; English slot and Dutch slot are cognates, the English t corresponding to German ss. [wiktionary]

herd.context_phrase: Der Topf steht auf dem Herd.
herd.context_translation: The pot is on the stove.
herd.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic herth; English hearth is a direct cognate, the English th corresponding to German d. [wiktionary]

ofen.context_phrase: Der Kuchen ist noch im Ofen.
ofen.context_translation: The cake is still in the oven.
ofen.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic ofn; English oven is a direct cognate from the same Germanic word, differing only in the vowel. [wiktionary]

waschmaschine.context_translation: The washing machine is running in the basement.
waschmaschine.etymology_derivation: Compound of waschen and Maschine; waschen is a direct cognate of English wash, and Maschine matches English machine, both from Latin machina. [wiktionary]

mikrowelle.context_phrase: Die Suppe ist in der Mikrowelle.
mikrowelle.context_translation: The soup is in the microwave.
mikrowelle.etymology_derivation: Compound of the Greek loan prefix mikro- and Welle, meaning wave; Mikro- is the same Greek element as English micro-. [wiktionary]

teller.etymology_derivation: From Middle French tailloir, meaning cutting board, from the Old French cutting verb tailler; English tailor descends from the same Old French verb. [wiktionary]

tasse.etymology_derivation: Via Middle French tasse from Arabic tas, meaning bowl, itself from Middle Persian tasht; English keeps the same word in the dialectal tass, while standard English uses cup. [wiktionary]

gabel.context_phrase: Ich esse den Salat mit der Gabel.
gabel.context_translation: I am eating the salad with the fork.
gabel.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic gabulu, meaning fork; English gable is the same Germanic word, naming the fork-shaped upper end of a house wall. [wiktionary]

messer.context_phrase: Schneide das Brot mit dem Messer.
messer.context_translation: Cut the bread with the knife.
messer.etymology_derivation: From Old High German mezzisahs, literally food knife; the first part is the food root behind English meat, the second the knife root behind English saw, with t appearing as ss in German. [wiktionary]

löffel.context_phrase: Nimm einen Löffel für die Suppe.
löffel.context_translation: Take a spoon for the soup.
löffel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic lapilaz, from the root lap, meaning to lick or lap; English lap is the related word, and its p appears as f in German. [wiktionary]

flasche.context_phrase: Die Flasche Wasser kostet zwei Euro.
flasche.context_translation: The bottle of water costs two euros.
flasche.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic flasko, from a root meaning to plait or braid, since bottles were once wrapped in straw; English flask is a direct cognate. [wiktionary]

topf.context_translation: The soup is cooking in the pot.
topf.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic duppaz, meaning hollow thing; the listed English cognate is dop, the diamond-cutter's cup, and the same PIE hollow root dewb gives English deep, with d becoming t in High German. [wiktionary]

becher.context_phrase: Ich trinke den Kakao aus einem Becher.
becher.context_translation: I am drinking the cocoa from a mug.
becher.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic bikari, borrowed from Latin bicarium, likely a diminutive of Greek bikos, meaning jar or amphora; English beaker is the same Latin loan. [wiktionary]

schüssel.context_phrase: Die Schüssel Salat steht auf dem Tisch.
schüssel.context_translation: The bowl of salad is on the table.
schüssel.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic skutilu, an early borrowing of Latin scutella, meaning shallow dish; English scuttle, as in coal scuttle, is the same Latin word through Old English. [wiktionary]

kanne.context_phrase: Die Kanne Tee ist noch heiß.
kanne.context_translation: The pot of tea is still hot.
kanne.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic kanno; English can is a direct cognate from Old English canne, originally meaning cup or vessel. [wiktionary]

dose.context_translation: The can is in the kitchen cabinet.
dose.etymology_derivation: Probably from Latin dosis via Middle Low German dose; the sense moved from a dose of medicine to the container that holds it, and English dose is the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

schale.context_phrase: Die Banane hat eine gelbe Schale.
schale.context_translation: The banana has a yellow peel.
schale.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic skalo, meaning husk or shell; English shell and shale are cognates from the same Germanic root. [wiktionary]

gewitter.context_phrase: Bei dem Gewitter bleiben wir drinnen.
gewitter.context_translation: During the thunderstorm we stay inside.
gewitter.etymology_derivation: Ge- plus Wetter (weather) — literally an intensified weather; from Proto-Germanic *gawidriją, the same root as English weather, which the page notes is distantly cognate in structure to English aweather. [wiktionary]

regenbogen.context_phrase: Nach dem Regen sehen wir einen Regenbogen.
regenbogen.context_translation: After the rain we see a rainbow.
regenbogen.etymology_derivation: Regen (rain) plus Bogen (bow — twin of English bow); the page lists English rainbow as the parallel cognate — the exact same compound. [wiktionary]

hagel.context_phrase: Der Hagel macht das Auto kaputt.
hagel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *haglaz — the exact twin of English hail (Old English hagol), confirmed on the English hail page, which names German Hagel as its cognate. No plural. [wiktionary]

hageln.etymology_derivation: Weak verb from Hagel (hail); the page compares Dutch hagelen and English hail (verb) directly — German weather verbs work like it rains: es regnet, es schneit, es hagelt. [wiktionary]

hitze.context_phrase: In der Hitze trinken wir viel Wasser.
hitze.context_translation: In the heat we drink lots of water.
hitze.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hitjǭ (heat); the page says cognate with Dutch hitte and related to English heat — the t-to-z shift shows between heat and Hitze. A cousin of the heiß-hot pair. [wiktionary]

kälte.context_phrase: Ich hasse die Kälte im Winter.
kälte.context_translation: I hate the cold in winter.
kälte.etymology_derivation: Kalt (cold) plus -e; kalt is the twin of English cold with English d become German t (the d-to-t shift); the page says perhaps comparable to English cold. [wiktionary]

wärme.context_phrase: Ich genieße die Wärme der Sonne.
wärme.context_translation: I enjoy the warmth of the sun.
wärme.etymology_derivation: Warm plus the noun suffix -e; warm is the identical twin of English warm (Proto-Germanic *warmaz), so die Wärme is simply warmness. [wiktionary]

frieren.context_translation: Are you cold? I am making tea.
frieren.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *freusaną — the page names English freeze as a cognate; the strong past fror, gefroren mirrors froze, frozen. The German infinitive r spread from the old past forms. [wiktionary]

schmelzen.context_phrase: Der Schnee schmilzt in der Sonne.
schmelzen.context_translation: The snow melts in the sun.
schmelzen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *smeltaną — the page names English smelt as the cognate, a twin variant of melt; strong verb class 3: schmolz, geschmolzen. [wiktionary]

tauen.context_phrase: Das Eis taut in der Sonne.
tauen.context_translation: The ice thaws in the sun.
tauen.etymology_derivation: Two old verbs merged in Middle High German: to dew (Proto-Germanic *dawwāną, the family of dew) and to thaw (Proto-West Germanic *þauwjan) — English thaw kept the th, German shifted it to d. [wiktionary]

schauer.context_phrase: Ein Schauer kommt, nimm den Regenschirm.
schauer.context_translation: A shower is coming, take the umbrella.
schauer.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skūrō — the page names English shower as a cognate (English palatalized sk to sh, German kept sch); German Schauer also means a shudder. [wiktionary]

sonnenuntergang.context_phrase: Wir sehen den Sonnenuntergang am Meer.
sonnenuntergang.context_translation: We watch the sunset at the sea.
sonnenuntergang.etymology_derivation: Sonne (sun) plus Untergang (down-going: unter under, Gang a going) — three Germanic twins in a row (sun, under, gang); literally sun-under-go, while English sunset rebuilt it with set. [wiktionary]

sonnenaufgang.context_phrase: Der Sonnenaufgang ist im Sommer früh.
sonnenaufgang.context_translation: The sunrise is early in summer.
sonnenaufgang.etymology_derivation: Sonne (sun) plus Aufgang (up-going; auf is the twin of up); the page cites the Old English twin sunnan upgang — the ancestor pattern of English sunrise. [wiktionary]

unwetter.context_phrase: Bei dem Unwetter bleibt das Flugzeug am Boden.
unwetter.context_translation: During the storm the plane stays on the ground.
unwetter.etymology_derivation: Un- (bad) plus Wetter (weather — twin of English weather); literally un-weather, severe weather. The page even names the fossil English twin unweather. [wiktionary]

jeans.context_phrase: Ich trage heute meine blaue Jeans.
jeans.context_translation: I am wearing my blue jeans today.
jeans.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English jeans (denim trousers) - a straight English loan. [wiktionary]

pullover.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English pull over, adopted with a spelling pronunciation. [wiktionary]

anzug.context_phrase: Er trägt einen schwarzen Anzug zur Arbeit.
anzug.context_translation: He wears a black suit to work.
anzug.etymology_derivation: an- + Zug (a pulling); Zug descends from Proto-Germanic *tugiz, the exact twin of English tug - the suit you pull on. [wiktionary]

bluse.context_phrase: Die Bluse ist weiß und die Hose ist schwarz.
bluse.context_translation: The blouse is white and the trousers are black.
bluse.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French blouse - the same French word that gave English blouse. [wiktionary]

kappe.context_phrase: Er setzt die Kappe auf den Kopf.
kappe.context_translation: He puts the cap on his head.
kappe.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German kappe, from Proto-West Germanic *kappā (coat, hood), a doublet of Kapuze - the same Late Latin cappa family as English cap. [wiktionary][etymonline]

krawatte.context_phrase: Im Büro trägt er Hemd und Krawatte.
krawatte.context_translation: At the office he wears a shirt and tie.
krawatte.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French cravate, a doublet of Kroate (Croat) - named for Croatian mercenaries; English cravat is the same word. [wiktionary]

uniform.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French uniforme, from Latin uniformis (uni- one + forma form); English uniform is the same borrowing. [wiktionary]

rucksack.context_phrase: Im Rucksack sind Wasser und Brot.
rucksack.context_translation: In the backpack there are water and bread.
rucksack.etymology_derivation: Rücken (back) + Sack (sack); English borrowed rucksack directly from German, and Sack itself is the same word in both languages. [wiktionary]

stoff.context_phrase: Dieser Stoff ist weich und billig.
stoff.context_translation: This fabric is soft and cheap.
stoff.etymology_derivation: Borrowed via Dutch from Old French estoffe - the same French word that gave English stuff; a Germanic root (stopfen) that traveled through French and came back. [wiktionary][etymonline]

leder.context_phrase: Meine Schuhe sind aus echtem Leder.
leder.context_translation: My shoes are made of real leather.
leder.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *leþrą (leather): English kept the ancient th, High German hardened it to d. [wiktionary]

wolle.context_phrase: Der Schal ist aus warmer Wolle.
wolle.context_translation: The scarf is made of warm wool.
wolle.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *wullu - the exact twin of English wool, from the PIE root *h₂welh₁- (wool). [wiktionary]

baumwolle.context_phrase: Dieses Hemd ist aus reiner Baumwolle.
baumwolle.context_translation: This shirt is made of pure cotton.
baumwolle.etymology_derivation: Baum (tree) + Wolle (wool): cotton, literally tree-wool - a name going back to Herodotus's tale of wool-bearing trees. [wiktionary]

ausziehen.english_cognate: to take off, to move out
ausziehen.english_meaning: to take off, to move out
ausziehen.context_phrase: Zuhause ziehe ich die Schuhe aus.
ausziehen.context_translation: At home I take off my shoes.
ausziehen.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + ziehen (to pull): aus is the t-to-s twin of English out, and the root is the *teuhaną of English tug. [wiktionary]

anprobieren.context_translation: I would like to try on the jacket.
anprobieren.etymology_derivation: an- + probieren (to try), from Latin probare - a verb of the French-derived -ieren family; as a separable verb it keeps ge- inside: anprobiert. [wiktionary]

passen.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French passer - the same French verb that gave English pass. [wiktionary][etymonline]

sandale.etymology_derivation: A 16th-century borrowing of Latin sandalium, from Greek sandalon, from Old Persian - the same Greek word that gave English sandal. [wiktionary][etymonline]

tragen.etymology_derivation: Class 6 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *draganą (to carry, drag) - the twin of English draw and drag; tragen-trug-getragen matches draw-drew-drawn. [wiktionary]

gummi.context_translation: The ball is made of rubber.
gummi.etymology_derivation: Borrowed in the 13th century from Medieval Latin gummi, from Greek kommi, ultimately Egyptian - the same chain that gave English gum. [wiktionary][etymonline]

körper.context_phrase: Der menschliche Körper hat viele Knochen.
körper.context_translation: The human body has many bones.
körper.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German korper, from Latin corpor-, the stem of corpus. English corpse is the direct cognate. [wiktionary]

lippe.context_phrase: Sie beißt sich auf die Lippe.
lippe.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German and northern Middle High German lippe, from Old High German *lippa, from Proto-West Germanic *lippjō, the same form behind English lip. [wiktionary]

kinn.context_phrase: Er hat einen kleinen Punkt am Kinn.
kinn.context_translation: He has a little spot on his chin.
kinn.etymology_derivation: From Old High German kinni, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from PIE *ǵénu- meaning jaw, cheek. English chin is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

ellbogen.context_phrase: Ich habe mir den Ellbogen gestoßen.
ellbogen.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German elenboge, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô, literally ell plus bow. English elbow is the same compound of the same two roots. [wiktionary]

muskel.etymology_derivation: A learned borrowing around 1700 from Latin musculus, the same Latin word that gave English muscle. [wiktionary]

nerv.context_phrase: Der Lärm geht mir auf die Nerven.
nerv.context_translation: The noise is getting on my nerves.
nerv.etymology_derivation: From Latin nervus, partly via French nerf. English nerve comes from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

rippe.context_phrase: Er hat sich eine Rippe gebrochen.
rippe.etymology_derivation: From Old High German rippa, from Proto-Germanic *ribją meaning rib, reef. English rib is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

lunge.context_phrase: Rauchen ist schlecht für die Lunge.
lunge.context_translation: Smoking is bad for the lungs.
lunge.etymology_derivation: From Old High German lunga, from Proto-Germanic *lungô, literally the light organ. English lung is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

träne.context_phrase: Eine Träne läuft ihr über das Gesicht.
träne.context_translation: A tear runs down her face.
träne.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German træne, from Old High German trahan, from Proto-West Germanic *trahnu. English tear is a cognate. [wiktionary]

bart.context_translation: My father wears a full beard.
bart.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bart, from Proto-Germanic *bardaz, from PIE *bʰardʰéh₂. English beard is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

brust.context_phrase: Sie hält das Baby an ihrer Brust.
brust.context_translation: She holds the baby to her breast.
brust.etymology_derivation: From Old High German brust, from Proto-West Germanic *brust, from Proto-Germanic *brusts. English breast continues the same Proto-Germanic word. [wiktionary]

augenbraue.etymology_derivation: A compound of Auge and Braue, from Middle High German ougenbrāwe. English brow is the cognate of Braue. [wiktionary]

hüfte.context_phrase: Sie legt die Hände auf die Hüften.
hüfte.context_translation: She puts her hands on her hips.
hüfte.etymology_derivation: From Old High German huf, from Proto-Germanic *hupiz. English hip is a listed cognate, keeping the old p where High German shifted to f. [wiktionary]

faust.context_phrase: Er ballt die Hand zur Faust.
faust.context_translation: He clenches his hand into a fist.
faust.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German fūst, from Old High German fūst. English fist is the regular English continuation of this same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

bluten.context_translation: The finger is bleeding a little.
bluten.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bluoten, from Proto-West Germanic *blōdijan, a verb from Blut. English bleed continues the same Proto-West Germanic verb. [wiktionary]

sterben.etymology_derivation: From Old High German stërban, from Proto-Germanic *sterbaną. English starve is the sole listed English cognate, once meaning simply to die. [wiktionary]

schweiß.context_phrase: Nach dem Sport tropft der Schweiß.
schweiß.context_translation: After exercise, the sweat is dripping.
schweiß.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sweiz, from Proto-Germanic *swaitaz. English sweat is a listed cognate, keeping the old t where High German shifted to ß. [wiktionary]

hören.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German hœren, from Old High German hōren. English hear is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

niesen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German niosan, from Proto-Germanic *hneusaną, a variant of *fneusaną. English sneeze is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

riechen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German riohhan, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. English reek is a listed cognate, keeping the k where German shifted to ch. [wiktionary]

hungrig.context_phrase: Die Kinder sind hungrig nach der Schule.
hungrig.context_translation: The children are hungry after school.
hungrig.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hungrugaz, by surface analysis Hunger plus -ig. English hungry is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

durstig.context_phrase: Nach dem Lauf bin ich durstig.
durstig.context_translation: After the run, I am thirsty.
durstig.etymology_derivation: Equivalent to Durst plus -ig. English thirsty carries the old th where the German base Durst has d. [wiktionary]

puls.etymology_derivation: From Late Middle High German puls, from Latin pulsus. English pulse comes from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

beißen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
beißen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bīȥan, from Proto-Germanic *bītaną. English bite is a listed cognate, with the same ablaut as bite bit bitten. [wiktionary]

lecken.etymology_derivation: From Old High German lecchōn, from Proto-Germanic *likkōną. English lick is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

schwitzen.context_translation: In summer, we sweat a lot.
schwitzen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German swizzen, from Proto-West Germanic *swittjan, from Proto-Germanic *switjaną. English sweat is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

knien.context_translation: He kneels next to the child.
knien.etymology_derivation: Inherited from Middle High German kniewen, by surface analysis Knie plus -en. English knee continues the same Proto-Germanic noun. [wiktionary]

tier.etymology_derivation: From Old High German tior, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from PIE *dʰewsóm. English deer is the listed cognate; the Germanic d appears as t in High German. [wiktionary]

haustier.context_phrase: Ein Hund ist ein beliebtes Haustier.
haustier.context_translation: A dog is a popular pet.
haustier.etymology_derivation: A compound of Haus and Tier, both direct cognates: house and deer, since Tier originally meant any animal. [wiktionary]

schaf.context_phrase: Das Schaf steht auf der Wiese.
schaf.context_translation: The sheep stands in the meadow.
schaf.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German schâf, from Old High German scāf, from Proto-Germanic *skapą. English sheep is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

hase.context_phrase: Der Hase springt über das Feld.
hase.context_translation: The hare jumps over the field.
hase.etymology_derivation: From Old High German haso, from Proto-West Germanic *hasō, from Proto-Germanic *hesô, from an old root meaning grey. English hare belongs to the same Germanic grey-word family. [wiktionary]

fuchs.context_translation: The fox sleeps in the forest.
fuchs.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fuhs, from Proto-Germanic *fuhsaz, from PIE *púḱsos, the tailed one. English fox is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

biene.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German bine, from Old High German bini, from Proto-West Germanic *bini. English bee is the cognate from the same bee-root. [wiktionary]

wespe.context_phrase: Eine Wespe sitzt auf dem Kuchen.
wespe.context_translation: A wasp sits on the cake.
wespe.etymology_derivation: From Old High German wefsa, from Proto-West Germanic *wapsu, from Proto-Germanic *wapsō, related to the verb web. English wasp is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

käfer.context_phrase: Ein kleiner Käfer krabbelt auf dem Blatt.
käfer.context_translation: A little beetle crawls on the leaf.
käfer.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German këvere, from Proto-West Germanic *kefrō. English chafer, as in cockchafer, is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

spinne.etymology_derivation: From Old High German spinna, an agent noun from the verb spinnen, to spin. Archaic English spinner is the listed cognate, and English spider is built on the same spin root. [wiktionary]

wurm.etymology_derivation: From Old High German wurm, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz, from PIE *wr̥mis. English worm is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

tiger.context_translation: The tiger lives in the jungle.
tiger.etymology_derivation: The German entry derives Tiger only from the earlier compound Tigertier and gives no older chain. The identity with English tiger, from Greek tigris, is assumed here and flagged for human check. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

eule.context_translation: The owl sleeps during the day.
eule.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German iule, from Old High German ūwila, from Proto-West Germanic *uwwulā, glossed owl. English owl continues the same West Germanic word. [wiktionary]

esel.etymology_derivation: From Old High German esil, from late Proto-West Germanic *asil, borrowed from Late Latin asellus, the diminutive of asinus behind English ass. [wiktionary]

ratte.context_phrase: Eine Ratte läuft durch den Keller.
ratte.context_translation: A rat runs through the cellar.
ratte.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ratta, from Proto-West Germanic *ratt, from Proto-Germanic *rattaz. English rat is the cognate. [wiktionary]

frosch.context_translation: The frog sits by the pond.
frosch.etymology_derivation: From Old High German frosk, from Proto-Germanic *fruskaz, from PIE *prew-, to jump. Dialectal English frosh is the listed cognate, and frog is named in the Bavarian section. [wiktionary]

schwan.context_phrase: Der Schwan schwimmt auf dem See.
schwan.context_translation: The swan swims on the lake.
schwan.etymology_derivation: From Old High German swan, from Proto-West Germanic *swan, from Proto-Germanic *swanaz, from PIE *swenh₂-, to sound. English swan is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

feder.context_phrase: Die Feder fällt langsam zu Boden.
feder.context_translation: The feather falls slowly to the ground.
feder.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fëdara, from Proto-West Germanic *feþru, from Proto-Germanic *feþrō, from PIE *péth₂r-, feather, wing. English feather is the listed cognate, keeping the th where German has d. [wiktionary]

fluss.context_phrase: Der Fluss fließt durch die Stadt.
fluss.context_translation: The river flows through the city.
fluss.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German vluȥ, from Proto-Germanic *flutiz, from the same root as fließen, to flow. English flow is the cognate of that root. [wiktionary]

see.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sē, from Proto-West Germanic *saiwi, from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz. English sea is the listed cognate; der See is the lake, die See the sea. [wiktionary]

bach.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bah, from Proto-West Germanic *baki. Northern English beck is the living cognate, keeping the k where German shifted to ch. [wiktionary]

teich.etymology_derivation: From Old High German tīh, from Proto-West Germanic *dīk, a doublet of Deich. English ditch and dike are the listed cognates, keeping the d where German shifted to t. [wiktionary]

meer.etymology_derivation: From Old High German meri, from Proto-West Germanic *mari. English mere is the listed cognate, and Latin mare is cognate through Indo-European. [wiktionary]

küste.etymology_derivation: From early modern Dutch kust, from Old French coste, from Latin costa, rib. English coast is the listed cognate from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

insel.context_translation: The island lies in the south.
insel.etymology_derivation: From Old High German isila, borrowed from Latin insula. English isle and insular come from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

berg.context_phrase: Der Berg ist im Winter weiß.
berg.context_translation: The mountain is white in winter.
berg.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bërg, from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz. English barrow, a burial hill, is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

feld.context_phrase: Der Bauer arbeitet auf dem Feld.
feld.context_translation: The farmer works in the field.
feld.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *felþuz: the p → f labial shift is the visible law; both languages independently hardened the old þ to d (field, Feld), so no dental shift separates them. [wiktionary]

welt.context_phrase: Die Welt ist groß und schön.
welt.context_translation: The world is big and beautiful.
welt.etymology_derivation: Inherited from Old High German wëralt, from Proto-West Germanic *weraldi, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz, literally the age of man. English world is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

wurzel.etymology_derivation: From Old High German wurzala, from Proto-Germanic *wurt- plus *waluz. Old English wyrtwalu and modern English wort, as in plant names, are the cognates. [wiktionary]

heide.context_translation: The heath blooms in late summer.
heide.etymology_derivation: From Old High German heida, from Proto-West Germanic *haiþi, from Proto-Germanic *haiþī. English heath is the listed cognate, keeping the th where German has d. [wiktionary]

busch.context_translation: The bird sits in the bush.
busch.etymology_derivation: From Old High German busk, from Proto-West Germanic *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz. English bush is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

zweig.context_phrase: Die Katze klettert auf den Zweig.
zweig.context_translation: The cat climbs onto the branch.
zweig.etymology_derivation: From Old High German zwīg, from Proto-Germanic *twīgą. English twig is the listed cognate, keeping the t where German shifted to z. [wiktionary]

moos.context_phrase: Das Moos wächst auf dem Stein.
moos.context_translation: The moss grows on the stone.
moos.etymology_derivation: From Old High German mos, from Proto-Germanic *musą. English moss is the cognate from the same Proto-Germanic word. [wiktionary]

buche.context_phrase: Die Buche ist hoch und alt.
buche.context_translation: The beech is tall and old.
buche.etymology_derivation: From Old High German buohha, from Proto-West Germanic *bōku and *bōkijā. English beech is the listed cognate; the entry also notes a possible link to Buch, book. [wiktionary]

birke.context_phrase: Die Birke hat eine weiße Rinde.
birke.etymology_derivation: From Old High German birka, from Proto-West Germanic *birkijā. English birch is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

auch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *auk — the same word as the archaic English eke 'also', as in to eke out; English let it fade, German kept auch. [wiktionary]

noch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nuh, from PIE *nu 'now' plus *-kʷe 'and, also' — literally and-now; the page lists no English cognate, but that first piece is the very 'now' element. [wiktionary]

schon.etymology_derivation: Originally the adverb of schön 'beautiful' (Middle High German schōne 'beautifully'); it slid to already, and the page compares English pretty making the same journey. [wiktionary]

nur.etymology_derivation: Contracted from Old High German niwāri, literally were it not (ni 'not' + wāri 'were'); Old English had the same word nǣre — from if-not to only. [wiktionary]

sehr.etymology_derivation: Old High German sēr 'injured, painful', from West Germanic *sair — the same word as English sore; both drifted from painfully to very, as English sorely shows. [wiktionary]

gerne.etymology_derivation: Variant of gern, from Proto-Germanic *gernaz 'eager, willing' — the same word as English yearn (Middle English yern, listed on the page); ich spiele gerne is literally I play yearningly. [wiktionary]

selten.etymology_derivation: West Germanic *seldanā — the twin of English seldom, which the page lists as a cognate; German hardened d into t (seld- to selt-). [wiktionary]

dann.etymology_derivation: The twin of English then: West Germanic *þan, which the page labels cognate with English then; English kept the th, German shifted it to d. [wiktionary]

vorher.etymology_derivation: A univerbation of vor 'before' + her 'ago, hither' — literally before-here, an everyday adverb built from two ancient words. [wiktionary]

wirklich.etymology_derivation: From wirken 'to act, take effect' + -lich: originally in a working, effective way, hence really. [wiktionary]

bestimmt.etymology_derivation: The past participle of bestimmen 'to determine': determined, fixed — hence the particle sense certainly. [wiktionary]

zusammen.etymology_derivation: zu 'to' + sammen 'together', from PIE *sem- 'one': Middle English had the same compound tosamen and obsolete English sam meant together — the classic English t to German z shift sits right in zu. [wiktionary]

allein.etymology_derivation: Middle High German al-ein, literally all one — the identical compound that formed English alone (Middle English al-one). [wiktionary]

alles.etymology_derivation: Old High German allaz, the neuter of all 'all' + -es: literally all of it. [wiktionary]

jeder.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ioweder (io 'ever' + wedar), the compound the page compares with English either; it originally meant each of two before merging with ieder. [wiktionary]

etwas.etymology_derivation: From Old High German eddeshwaz: edde- (probably the old word behind oder 'or') + hwaz 'what' — originally something like or-what, hence something. [wiktionary]

nichts.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German nihtes niht, literally nothing of nothing — an emphatic doubling of niht 'not', just like French rien de rien. [wiktionary]

niemand.etymology_derivation: nie 'never' + Mann 'man': literally never-man — the page analyzes it exactly so, the same idea as English no man and none. [wiktionary]

wieder.context_translation: We will see each other again.
wieder.etymology_derivation: Old High German widar 'against', from West Germanic *wiþr 'toward, against' — the page names English wither and widdershins as cognates; German wieder turned against into again. [wiktionary]

echt.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German echt 'lawful, genuine', from ē 'law' — related to German Ehe 'marriage', the lawful bond; English uses echt as a loan from German. [wiktionary]

ganz.etymology_derivation: West Germanic *gant 'whole, sound' — Middle High German ganz meant whole and healthy; no English cognate is listed on the page. [wiktionary]

einmal.context_phrase: Einmal im Jahr fahre ich ans Meer.
einmal.context_translation: Once a year I go to the sea.
einmal.etymology_derivation: ein 'one' + Mal 'time': Middle High German einmāle — literally one-time, hence once. [wiktionary]

einige.context_phrase: Einige Leute warten vor dem Kino.
einige.context_translation: Some people are waiting in front of the cinema.
einige.etymology_derivation: Inflected form of einig, from ein (the exact twin of English one, Proto-Germanic *ainaz) plus the -ig suffix; some, a few. [wiktionary]

beide.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *bai, the ancient Germanic dual meaning both, two; the same root grew into English both, which fused it with a demonstrative. [wiktionary]

sonst.context_phrase: Beeil dich, sonst kommen wir zu spät.
sonst.context_translation: Hurry up, otherwise we will be too late.
sonst.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sus (thus), Proto-West Germanic *sus, from the ancient root *swa that also gives English so; the sense drifted from thus to otherwise. [wiktionary]

leider.context_phrase: Leider ist das Museum heute geschlossen.
leider.context_translation: Unfortunately the museum is closed today.
leider.etymology_derivation: Originally the comparative of leid (grievous, as in es tut mir leid, I am sorry) — literally more grievously, now simply unfortunately. [wiktionary]

überall.context_translation: I am looking everywhere for my glasses.
überall.etymology_derivation: Über (twin of English over — English v became German b) plus all (twin of all); the page itself says compare English overall. [wiktionary]

irgendwo.context_phrase: Mein Handy ist irgendwo im Haus.
irgendwo.context_translation: My phone is somewhere in the house.
irgendwo.etymology_derivation: Irgend (any, at all) plus wo (where, the twin of English where); literally anywhere, that is somewhere. [wiktionary]

doch.english_cognate: yet; after all (particle: on the contrary)
doch.english_meaning: yet; after all (particle: on the contrary)
doch.context_phrase: Das Essen war teuer, doch sehr lecker.
doch.context_translation: The food was expensive, yet very tasty.
doch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *þauh — the exact twin of English though (Old English þēah); English kept th, German hardened it to d, the classic dental shift. [wiktionary]

mehrere.etymology_derivation: Mehrere is mehr (more — the exact twin of English more) plus -ere; a German-internal formation meaning several. [wiktionary]

eigentlich.etymology_derivation: Eigen (twin of English own) plus -lich (twin of -ly) — originally ownly, in truth, now mainly actually; inherited from Middle High German eigenliche. [wiktionary]

obwohl.context_phrase: Ich gehe laufen, obwohl es regnet.
obwohl.context_translation: I go running although it rains.
obwohl.etymology_derivation: Univerbation of ob (whether) and wohl (well — twin of English well); literally whether-well, hence although. English although is unrelated; the value here is the sentence-building role. [wiktionary]

damit.context_phrase: Ich lerne Deutsch, damit ich in Berlin arbeiten kann.
damit.context_translation: I am learning German so that I can work in Berlin.
damit.etymology_derivation: Da (there — the th-to-d twin of English there) plus mit (with, twin of with); the page itself compares English therewith. As a conjunction: so that. [wiktionary]

während.etymology_derivation: Originally the present participle of währen (to last — the page traces it to PIE *h₂wes-, the root of English was), later rebracketed into a preposition; English during and while are unrelated. [wiktionary]

trotzdem.context_phrase: Es war kalt, trotzdem schwammen wir.
trotzdem.context_translation: It was cold, nevertheless we swam.
trotzdem.etymology_derivation: Trotz (defiance, Middle High German truz) plus dem (that — the th-to-d twin of the/that); literally despite that. English nevertheless is unrelated; the B1 value is its sentence-building role. [wiktionary]

deshalb.context_phrase: Es regnete, deshalb blieben wir zu Hause.
deshalb.context_translation: It rained, therefore we stayed at home.
deshalb.etymology_derivation: Des (genitive of das, twin of the/that) plus halb (side, half — twin of English half, where English f became German b); literally of that side, therefore. [wiktionary]

falls.context_phrase: Falls es regnet, bleibe ich hier.
falls.context_translation: In case it rains, I stay here.
falls.etymology_derivation: Presumably the genitive of Fall (case, fall — exact twin of English fall); in the case of a fall, that is in case. [wiktionary]

sondern.context_phrase: Das ist nicht mein Buch, sondern deins.
sondern.context_translation: That is not my book but yours.
sondern.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *sundraz (apart); the page names English sunder as a straight cognate — nicht X, sondern Y means not X but rather Y. [wiktionary]

hoffentlich.etymology_derivation: Hoffen (to hope — twin of English hope, where English p became German pf) plus -lich (twin of -ly); hopefully. [wiktionary]

außerdem.etymology_derivation: Außer (outside of, built on aus — out, twin of English out) plus dem (that); literally besides that. English besides is unrelated. [wiktionary]

dennoch.context_phrase: Sie ist müde, dennoch lernt sie weiter.
dennoch.context_translation: She is tired, nevertheless she keeps studying.
dennoch.etymology_derivation: Denn (then — the th-to-d twin of English then) plus noch (still, yet); literally then-yet, nevertheless. [wiktionary]

zwar.context_phrase: Das Auto ist zwar alt, aber schnell.
zwar.context_translation: The car is admittedly old but fast.
zwar.etymology_derivation: A contraction of Old High German zi ware: zu (the t-to-z twin of English to) plus wahr (true); literally to-truth, indeed, admittedly. [wiktionary]

seitdem.context_phrase: Seitdem ich hier wohne, fahre ich Rad.
seitdem.context_translation: Since I live here, I cycle.
seitdem.etymology_derivation: Seit (since) plus dem (that — the th-to-d twin of the/that); literally since-that, since then, as adverb and conjunction. [wiktionary]

krankenhaus.context_translation: My uncle works at the hospital.
krankenhaus.etymology_derivation: Kranken (sick person) plus Haus (house — exact twin of English house, Proto-Germanic *hūsą); the sick house. English hospital is a Latin word, unrelated. [wiktionary]

apotheke.context_phrase: Ich hole das Rezept in der Apotheke.
apotheke.context_translation: I get the prescription at the pharmacy.
apotheke.etymology_derivation: Ultimately from Ancient Greek apothēkē (storehouse) — the same Greek word that gave English apothecary, twin borrowings; German doublets are Boutique and Bodega. [wiktionary]

rezept.context_phrase: Der Arzt schreibt mir ein Rezept.
rezept.context_translation: The doctor writes me a prescription.
rezept.etymology_derivation: From earlier recept, from Latin receptus; the page states it is cognate with English receipt — recipe is just the cooking variant of the same word. [wiktionary]

unfall.context_phrase: Er hatte einen Unfall mit dem Fahrrad.
unfall.context_translation: He had an accident with the bicycle.
unfall.etymology_derivation: Un- (bad) plus Fall (case, fall — exact twin of English fall); literally a bad case, an accident. English accident is Latin, unrelated. [wiktionary]

krankheit.etymology_derivation: Krank (sick) plus -heit (-ness); the suffix -heit is the twin of English -hood (both Proto-Germanic *haiduz), so structurally sick-hood. [wiktionary]

tablette.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French tablette, from the same French-Latin word family as English tablet; a pill pressed into a little tablet. [wiktionary]

pille.context_phrase: Die Pille liegt auf dem Tisch.
pille.context_translation: The pill is lying on the table.
pille.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German pille, from Latin pilula (little ball) — the same Latin word behind English pill. [wiktionary]

retten.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hradjaną (to save); the page names English redd (dialectal, to put right) and everyday rid as cognates — to rid someone of danger is to rescue them. [wiktionary]

notruf.context_phrase: Im Notruf sagt man Name und Adresse.
notruf.context_translation: In the emergency call you say name and address.
notruf.etymology_derivation: Not (need, distress — twin of English need, Proto-Germanic *naudiz) plus Ruf (call); literally need-call — dial 112 or 110. [wiktionary]

telefonnummer.context_translation: I write down my phone number.
telefonnummer.etymology_derivation: Telefon plus Nummer (number — Latin numerus, the same word behind English number); Telefon is the same Greek-built international word as telephone. [wiktionary]

adresse.etymology_derivation: An unadapted borrowing from French adresse — the same French word that gives English address (ultimately Latin ad plus directum, made straight). [wiktionary]

unterschreiben.etymology_derivation: A Middle High German calque of Latin subscribere — under-write; unter is the twin of English under, and schreiben is the Latin-loan twin of scribe (English write is the native sibling). [wiktionary]

krankenwagen.etymology_derivation: Kranken (sick person) plus Wagen (car, wagon — exact twin of English wagon, Proto-Germanic *wagnaz); the sick wagon. English ambulance is French, unrelated. [wiktionary]

notfall.context_phrase: Im Notfall drücken Sie die Taste.
notfall.context_translation: In an emergency press the button.
notfall.etymology_derivation: Not (need, distress — twin of English need) plus Fall (case, fall — twin of English fall); literally need-fall, an emergency. [wiktionary]

rettung.context_phrase: Die Rettung kommt in zehn Minuten.
rettung.context_translation: The rescue comes in ten minutes.
rettung.etymology_derivation: Retten (to rescue) plus -ung, the twin of the English verbal-noun suffix -ing (Old English spelled it -ung); literally a rescuing. [wiktionary]

beruf.etymology_derivation: Literally the calling, deverbal of berufen (to call) - the same idea as English vocation (Latin vocare, to call), though the words are unrelated. [wiktionary]

soldat.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian soldato - literally one who receives soldo (pay), from the Latin gold coin solidus; the same coin that names the English soldier. [wiktionary][etymonline]

pilot.etymology_derivation: Borrowed about 1500 from Italian pilota, partly via French pilote - the same Italian word that gave English pilot. [wiktionary][etymonline]

mechaniker.etymology_derivation: Mechanik (mechanics) + -er; Mechanik is from Latin mechanicus, from Greek mekhanē (device) - the same Latin word as English mechanic. [wiktionary][etymonline]

fischer.context_phrase: Der Fischer fährt früh aufs Meer.
fischer.context_translation: The fisherman goes out to sea early.
fischer.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German vischære, from Proto-Germanic *fiskārijaz - the exact twin of the English surname Fisher (fish + -er). [wiktionary]

musiker.etymology_derivation: Musik + -er; Musik comes from Latin musica - the same Latin word behind English music and musician. [wiktionary][etymonline]

schauspieler.context_phrase: Der Schauspieler steht auf der Bühne.
schauspieler.context_translation: The actor stands on the stage.
schauspieler.etymology_derivation: Schauspiel + -er - literally a show-player; Schau is the same old word as English show (Proto-Germanic *skawwōną, Old English sceawian). [wiktionary]

professor.context_phrase: Der Professor unterrichtet an der Universität.
professor.context_translation: The professor teaches at the university.
professor.etymology_derivation: A learned borrowing of Latin professor (one who declares publicly); English professor is the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

direktor.context_translation: The principal works in the office.
direktor.etymology_derivation: From Latin director, the agent noun of dirigere (to guide straight); English director is from the same Latin verb. [wiktionary][etymonline]

sekretärin.etymology_derivation: Sekretär (secretary) + -in; Sekretär is borrowed from Latin secretarius (keeper of secrets) - the same Latin word as English secretary. [wiktionary][etymonline]

zahnarzt.context_translation: The dentist looks at my teeth.
zahnarzt.etymology_derivation: Zahn (tooth) + Arzt (doctor) - literally tooth-doctor; Zahn shows the t-to-z shift from the same ancient root as English tooth (PIE *h₃dónts). [wiktionary]

rentner.context_phrase: Der Rentner geht jeden Tag spazieren.
rentner.context_translation: The pensioner goes for a walk every day.
rentner.etymology_derivation: Rente (pension) + -ner; Rente is borrowed from Old French rente, from Medieval Latin rendita - the same source as English rent. [wiktionary][etymonline]

apotheker.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German apotēker, from Latin apothecarius (storekeeper) - the very word that became English apothecary. [wiktionary][etymonline]

krankenschwester.etymology_derivation: Kranker (ill one) + Schwester (sister) - a sick sister; Schwester is the exact twin of English sister (PIE *swésōr). [wiktionary]

autor.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from New Latin autor, from Latin auctor - compare English author and French auteur, all the same word. [wiktionary]

verdienen.context_translation: She earns a lot of money.
verdienen.etymology_derivation: From ver- + dienen (to serve), a calque of Latin deservio - the same Latin verb that gave English deserve (via Old French deservir). [wiktionary][etymonline]

kellner.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin cellenarius (cellarer), from Late Latin cellarium - the pantry word that also gave German Keller and English cellar. [wiktionary][etymonline]

handwerker.etymology_derivation: Hand (hand) + Werker (worker); Werk comes from Proto-Germanic *werką (PIE *wérǵom) - the exact ch-twin of English work. [wiktionary][etymonline]

elektriker.etymology_derivation: elektrisch (electric) + -er; elektrisch is from Neo-Latin electricus, coined by William Gilbert from Greek elektron (amber) - the stone where static electricity was first noticed; English electric is the same coinage. [wiktionary][etymonline]

sekunde.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin secunda, short for pars minuta secunda, the second small part of the hour — the same Latin phrase behind English second. [wiktionary]

mittag.context_phrase: Wir essen um zwölf Uhr zu Mittag.
mittag.context_translation: We eat lunch at twelve o'clock.
mittag.etymology_derivation: Mitt(e) + Tag, literally middle-day — the exact structural twin of English midday; Tag is the twin of day (d → t). [wiktionary]

mitternacht.etymology_derivation: Mitter + Nacht — inherited from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts, the very same middle-night compound as English midnight. [wiktionary]

wochenende.context_phrase: Am Wochenende fahren wir an den See.
wochenende.context_translation: On the weekend we go to the lake.
wochenende.etymology_derivation: Woche + Ende — the modern compound arose in the 19th century as a calque of English weekend; Woche is the twin of week (k → ch) and Ende the twin of end. [wiktionary]

feiertag.context_phrase: Heute ist ein Feiertag, alles ist zu.
feiertag.context_translation: Today is a public holiday, everything is closed.
feiertag.etymology_derivation: Feier + Tag — literally celebration day; Tag is the twin of day (d → t). [wiktionary]

ferien.context_phrase: Im Sommer haben wir sechs Wochen Ferien.
ferien.context_translation: In summer we have six weeks of holidays.
ferien.etymology_derivation: Plural-only word from Latin feriae, days of rest and festival, with the Latin plural ending replaced by German -en. [wiktionary]

termin.context_phrase: Ich habe morgen einen Termin beim Zahnarzt.
termin.context_translation: I have a dentist appointment tomorrow.
termin.etymology_derivation: From Latin terminus, boundary or limit — the same Latin word that gives English term and terminus. [wiktionary]

kalender.context_phrase: Ich schreibe den Termin in meinen Kalender.
kalender.context_translation: I write the appointment in my calendar.
kalender.etymology_derivation: From Latin calendārium — the same Latin word that gives English calendar. [wiktionary]
