wecker.context_phrase: Mein Wecker klingelt um sechs Uhr.
wecker.context_translation: My alarm clock rings at six o'clock.
wecker.etymology_derivation: wecken, to wake, + the agent suffix -er — literally a waker. [wiktionary]

anfang.context_translation: At the beginning it was hard.
anfang.etymology_derivation: an + Fang, catch — from anfangen, to catch at and so to begin; the entry lists archaic English fang, to seize, as a cognate. [wiktionary]

ende.context_phrase: Am Ende des Films weine ich immer.
ende.context_translation: At the end of the film I always cry.
ende.etymology_derivation: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *andijaz — the same root as English end. [wiktionary]

zuerst.context_phrase: Zuerst frühstücken wir, dann gehen wir.
zuerst.context_translation: First we have breakfast, then we go.
zuerst.etymology_derivation: zu + erst — zu is the twin of to (t → z) and erst the Germanic earliest, kept in archaic English erstwhile. [wiktionary]

uhrzeit.etymology_derivation: Uhr + Zeit — clock-time; Zeit is the twin of English tide, which originally meant time, as in eventide. [wiktionary]

abends.context_translation: In the evenings I read a book.
abends.etymology_derivation: Abend + adverbial -s, from an old adverbial genitive — the twin formation of the English adverb evenings. [wiktionary]

morgens.context_translation: In the mornings I drink coffee.
morgens.etymology_derivation: Morgen + adverbial -s, from an old adverbial genitive — the twin formation of the English adverb mornings. [wiktionary]

nachts.context_phrase: Nachts ist es hier ganz still.
nachts.context_translation: At night it is completely quiet here.
nachts.etymology_derivation: Nacht + adverbial -s — the entry lists the English adverb nights as a cognate; Nacht is night with gh → ch. [wiktionary]

mittags.context_translation: At midday we eat a hot meal.
mittags.etymology_derivation: Mittag + adverbial -s — literally at midday; Mittag is the structural twin of English midday. [wiktionary]

datum.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin datum, literally something given — the same Latin participle that gave English date, from the Roman letter formula given at Rome. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

übermorgen.context_translation: The day after tomorrow I am going to Berlin.
übermorgen.etymology_derivation: über + morgen — the exact structural twin of the archaic English adverb overmorrow, which Wiktionary records as a calque of this German word. [wiktionary]

vorgestern.context_translation: The day before yesterday the weather was better.
vorgestern.etymology_derivation: vor + gestern — literally fore-yesterday, the twin structure of the archaic English adverb ereyesterday; gestern is the y → g twin of yesterday. [wiktionary]

mittwoch.etymology_derivation: Mitte + Woche — literally mid-week; the entry cites English midweek as the cognate compound and notes it calqued Latin media hebdomas. [wiktionary]

werktag.context_phrase: An Werktagen stehen wir früh auf.
werktag.context_translation: On workdays we get up early.
werktag.etymology_derivation: Werk + Tag — the exact structural twin of workday; Werk is the twin of work (k → ch) and Tag the twin of day (d → t). [wiktionary]

bus.context_phrase: Der Bus kommt um acht Uhr.
bus.context_translation: The bus comes at eight o'clock.
bus.etymology_derivation: From Omnibus, the Latin for-all vehicle, shortened with influence from English bus — both languages took the same Latin dative. [wiktionary]

u-bahn.context_phrase: Ich nehme die U-Bahn zur Arbeit.
u-bahn.context_translation: I take the underground to work.
u-bahn.etymology_derivation: Short for Untergrundbahn, the underground railway: unter (under), Grund (ground, with the English d become German t), Bahn (railway). [wiktionary]

fahrrad.etymology_derivation: fahren (to drive, the fare root) + Rad (wheel): the driving-wheel. [wiktionary]

flugzeug.etymology_derivation: Flug (flight, from fliegen — English fly) + Zeug (gear, as in Feuerzeug): the fly-gear. [wiktionary]

taxi.context_phrase: Wir nehmen ein Taxi zum Hotel.
taxi.context_translation: We take a taxi to the hotel.
taxi.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French taxi, the cab named for its taximeter — the identical French word English uses. [wiktionary]

fahrkarte.context_phrase: Ich kaufe eine Fahrkarte nach Berlin.
fahrkarte.context_translation: I buy a ticket to Berlin.
fahrkarte.etymology_derivation: fahren (to travel, the fare root) + Karte (card, from Latin charta — the same loan as English card): a travel-card. [wiktionary]

koffer.etymology_derivation: Through Middle Dutch from Old French cofre — the French loan English also took as coffer and coffin. [wiktionary]

pass.etymology_derivation: From Old French pas, from Latin passus (step); the passport sense is a shortening of French passeport, the same source English used. [wiktionary]

dorf.context_phrase: Das Dorf liegt hinter dem Berg.
dorf.context_translation: The village lies behind the mountain.
dorf.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *thurpa — Old English thorp, which survives in English place names like Mablethorpe; the English th hardened into German d. [wiktionary]

strand.context_translation: We are going to the beach.
strand.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *strando — the page lists English strand (shore) as the direct cognate, as in London's Strand. [wiktionary]

karte.context_phrase: Ich brauche eine Karte für die U-Bahn.
karte.context_translation: I need a ticket for the underground.
karte.etymology_derivation: From Latin charta through Old French carte — the page compares English card: the same paper-word, borrowed in both languages. [wiktionary]

abfahrt.context_phrase: Die Abfahrt ist um neun Uhr.
abfahrt.context_translation: The departure is at nine o'clock.
abfahrt.etymology_derivation: The noun of abfahren: ab (off) + Fahrt (the fare root) — literally an off-driving, a departure. [wiktionary]

ankunft.context_phrase: Die Ankunft ist um halb sieben.
ankunft.context_translation: The arrival is at half past six.
ankunft.etymology_derivation: From ankommen (to arrive) — an on-coming; kommen is the German twin of come. [wiktionary]

abfahren.etymology_derivation: ab (off) + fahren (to drive): to drive off — the same verb root as English fare. [wiktionary]

ankommen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *anakwemana, to come to — an + kommen, with archaic English oncome as the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

einsteigen.context_phrase: Wir steigen in den Bus ein.
einsteigen.etymology_derivation: ein (in) + steigen (to climb): to climb in — German pictures boarding as climbing aboard; the climb-verb is native German. [wiktionary]

aussteigen.context_phrase: Ich steige an der nächsten Station aus.
aussteigen.context_translation: I get off at the next stop.
aussteigen.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + steigen (to climb): to climb out and off the train, bus or tram. [wiktionary]

haltestelle.context_translation: The bus stop is right here.
haltestelle.etymology_derivation: halten (to hold) + Stelle (place, from the same old place-root as English stall): a hold-place, where the vehicle stops. [wiktionary]

fähre.context_phrase: Die Fähre fährt über den Fluss.
fähre.context_translation: The ferry goes across the river.
fähre.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *farjo, the ferrying word of the same far-root as fahren — the page lists English ferry as cognate. [wiktionary]

tourist.context_phrase: Der Tourist fragt nach dem Weg.
tourist.context_translation: The tourist asks for the way.
tourist.etymology_derivation: Tour (tour, turn) + -ist; the page says it was formed in the 18th century, possibly influenced by English tourist being made at the same time from the same French material. [wiktionary]

ausflug.context_phrase: Wir machen einen Ausflug in die Berge.
ausflug.context_translation: We take a trip to the mountains.
ausflug.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + Flug (flight, from fliegen — English fly): literally an out-flight, an excursion. [wiktionary]

gepäck.context_phrase: Mein Gepäck ist noch nicht da.
gepäck.context_translation: My luggage is not here yet.
gepäck.etymology_derivation: A collective of Pack (bundle) — the Low German packing word English also took as pack. [wiktionary]

rezeption.context_phrase: Der Schlüssel ist an der Rezeption.
rezeption.context_translation: The key is at the reception desk.
rezeption.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin receptio — the same reception-word English uses for the hotel desk; both go back to the root of seize. [wiktionary]

spazieren.english_cognate: to stroll, go for a walk
spazieren.english_meaning: to stroll, go for a walk
spazieren.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian spaziare, from Latin spatiari, to stroll — an -ieren verb; English space is from the same Latin spatium. [wiktionary]

hafen.context_translation: The ship is lying in the harbor.
hafen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *habno — the page lists English haven as the direct cognate: a harbor is a haven. [wiktionary]

brücke.context_phrase: Die alte Brücke ist aus Stein.
brücke.context_translation: The old bridge is made of stone.
brücke.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *bruggju — the page lists English bridge as the cognate; German keeps the hard k where English softened to dg. [wiktionary]

fahrplan.context_phrase: Der Fahrplan hängt an der Wand.
fahrplan.context_translation: The timetable hangs on the wall.
fahrplan.etymology_derivation: fahren (to drive, the fare root) + Plan (plan, the same French-Latin word English uses): the travel-plan, a timetable. [wiktionary]

name.etymology_derivation: From Old High German namo, Proto-West Germanic *namō, the exact twin of English name. [wiktionary]

vorname.context_translation: Her first name is Maria Keller.
vorname.etymology_derivation: vor + Name, the exact calque of English forename. [wiktionary]

stiefvater.etymology_derivation: stief- (step-) + Vater; Proto-West Germanic *steupafadēr, the exact twin of English stepfather. [wiktionary]

stiefmutter.etymology_derivation: stief- (step-) + Mutter, twin of English stepmother; the stief-/step- prefix pair is the same *steupa- root verified under Stiefvater. [wiktionary]

braut.context_phrase: Die Braut trägt ein weißes Kleid.
braut.context_translation: The bride wears a white dress.
braut.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *brūdiz, Old High German brūt, the exact twin of English bride. [wiktionary]

hochzeit.etymology_derivation: hoch + Zeit, literally high time or high festival (Old High German hohun giziti); the Zeit element is the twin of English tide, as documented in the dictionary Zeit row. [wiktionary]

geburtstag.etymology_derivation: Geburt + Tag, exactly English birthday; the Tag/day pair shows the d to t stop shift, and Geburt comes from the gebären family. [wiktionary]

geboren.context_translation: I was born in Berlin in 1990.
geboren.etymology_derivation: Past participle of gebären, a class 4 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *gaberaną, cognate with English bear; geboren matches the participle born of the same ablaut series. [wiktionary]

schwiegervater.etymology_derivation: Schwieger- + Vater; the Vater element is the twin of English father (th to d, from PIE *ph₂tḗr). The old element Schwieger- has no surviving English twin. [wiktionary]

witwe.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *widuwǭ, Old High German wituwa, the twin of English widow, which comes from Old English widuwe. [wiktionary]

hoffnung.etymology_derivation: hoffen (to hope) + -ung: German hardened English p into pf-f, so hope became hoffen; the page lists English hoping as the cognate. [wiktionary]

wut.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wodaz, furious — Old English wode, mad: the English d became German t (like day and Tag), and Wednesday keeps the raging name. [wiktionary]

ärger.etymology_derivation: Back-formation from ärgern — from arg, bad; the verb page compares English eerie, from the same old Germanic bad-fearful root. [wiktionary]

ärgern.etymology_derivation: From arg, bad — the page compares English eerie, its cousin from the same Germanic root for fearful. [wiktionary]

sorge.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *surgo — the page lists English sorrow as the cognate: the same care-root that grew into sorrow. [wiktionary]

hass.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hatis — English hate with its t became German Hass with the shifted ss, just like water became Wasser. [wiktionary]

mut.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *modaz — the page lists English mood as the cognate: the English d became German t (day and Tag), and courage is having the right mood. [wiktionary]

langeweile.etymology_derivation: lang (long) + Weile (while — the exact English cognate): boredom is a long while. [wiktionary]

interesse.context_phrase: Sie zeigt großes Interesse an Musik.
interesse.context_translation: She shows great interest in music.
interesse.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin interesse, what lies between — the same Latin source as English interest. [wiktionary]

meinung.context_phrase: Meiner Meinung nach ist der Film gut.
meinung.context_translation: In my opinion the film is good.
meinung.etymology_derivation: meinen (to mean) + -ung; the page compares English meaning — your opinion is what you mean. [wiktionary]

gefühl.context_phrase: Ich habe ein gutes Gefühl dabei.
gefühl.context_translation: I have a good feeling about it.
gefühl.etymology_derivation: ge- + fühlen (to feel — the English feel twin): a feeling is a felt thing. [wiktionary]

stimmung.context_phrase: Die Stimmung auf der Party war super.
stimmung.context_translation: The mood at the party was great.
stimmung.etymology_derivation: stimmen (to be right, to tune) + -ung: your mood is the tuning of your inner instrument. [wiktionary]

heimweh.context_phrase: Nach einer Woche hatte sie Heimweh.
heimweh.context_translation: After a week she was homesick.
heimweh.etymology_derivation: Heim (home, Proto-Germanic *haimaz) + Weh (pain, from the root behind English woe): home-woe, homesickness. [wiktionary]

überraschung.context_phrase: Das Geschenk war eine große Überraschung.
überraschung.context_translation: The gift was a big surprise.
überraschung.etymology_derivation: From überraschen, to come at someone too quickly — its rasch (quick) is cognate with English rash. [wiktionary]

vertrauen.context_translation: Trust is more important than money.
vertrauen.etymology_derivation: ver + trauen (to trust): the same Germanic trust-root as archaic English trow, to believe. [wiktionary]

vermissen.etymology_derivation: ver + missen (to miss): to miss through and through — the missen root pairs with English miss. [wiktionary]

wünschen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wunskijana — the page lists English wish as the direct cognate, both from the wish-love root *wen. [wiktionary]

wunsch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wunska — the page lists English wish among the cognates; the verb is wünschen. [wiktionary]

scham.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skamo — the page lists English shame as the direct cognate: the same word, sound for sound. [wiktionary]

laden.context_phrase: Der Laden um die Ecke ist billig.
laden.context_translation: The shop around the corner is cheap.
laden.etymology_derivation: Originally the board or shutter of a market stall, then the stall itself — the page notes it is akin to English lath, a thin board. [wiktionary]

geschäft.context_phrase: Das Geschäft öffnet um neun Uhr.
geschäft.context_translation: The shop opens at nine o'clock.
geschäft.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *gaskafti, a doing of the schaffen (to make) family — the root whose English twin is shape, as the schaffen page lists. [wiktionary]

supermarkt.context_translation: I buy fruit at the supermarket.
supermarkt.etymology_derivation: super- (above) + Markt (market): the super- is the same Latin prefix English uses, and Markt is the market twin. [wiktionary]

tüte.etymology_derivation: From Low German tute, a conical bag — the page lists English tote as the cognate: the bag you tote things in. [wiktionary]

paket.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French paquet — the same French bundle-word behind English packet. [wiktionary]

zeitung.context_phrase: Er liest jeden Morgen die Zeitung.
zeitung.context_translation: He reads the newspaper every morning.
zeitung.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *tidungu, a message on the time-root — the page lists English tiding as the cognate: a Zeitung brings your tidings. [wiktionary]

zeitschrift.context_phrase: Die Zeitschrift liegt auf dem Tisch.
zeitschrift.context_translation: The magazine is lying on the table.
zeitschrift.etymology_derivation: Zeit (time) + Schrift (writing, from schreiben — the scribe-root): writings of the time, a periodical. [wiktionary]

prozent.context_phrase: Die Miete steigt um fünf Prozent.
prozent.context_translation: The rent rises by five percent.
prozent.etymology_derivation: From Italian per cento, Latin for by the hundred — the page confirms the same construction as English percent. [wiktionary]

münze.context_phrase: Ich habe nur eine Münze dabei.
münze.context_translation: I only have one coin with me.
münze.etymology_derivation: Through Proto-West Germanic *munit from Latin moneta, the coin-word that also became English money and mint. [wiktionary]

schein.context_translation: He pays with a ten-euro note.
schein.etymology_derivation: From the scheinen (shine) family — the page lists English shine as cognate; a banknote is literally a shine, what glints in the hand. [wiktionary]

kreditkarte.context_translation: I pay with the credit card.
kreditkarte.etymology_derivation: Kredit (credit, from Latin creditum, entrusted) + Karte (card, from Latin charta): the loan twins of English credit card. [wiktionary]

konto.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian conto, a calculation — the Latin counting-word behind English account. [wiktionary]

bank.context_translation: I am going to the bank.
bank.etymology_derivation: The money-changers bench: Bank is the Germanic twin of English bench (Proto-Germanic *bankiz), and the financial sense came through Italian banca. [wiktionary]

post.context_phrase: Ich bringe das Paket zur Post.
post.context_translation: I am taking the package to the post office.
post.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian posta, the relay-station word from Latin positus (placed) — the same post English uses for mail; German kept a pf-twin, Pfosten. [wiktionary]

bäckerei.etymology_derivation: Bäcker (baker, from backen — English bake) + -ei, the place suffix: the bake-house. [wiktionary]

kostenlos.etymology_derivation: Kosten (costs) + -los (free of); the page itself compares English costless — free of cost. [wiktionary]

angebot.context_translation: The offer is only valid today.
angebot.etymology_derivation: From anbieten, to offer — the old noun Bot is the Germanic twin of English bid: an offer is an up-bid. [wiktionary]

quittung.context_phrase: Können Sie mir eine Quittung geben?
quittung.context_translation: Can you give me a receipt?
quittung.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German quiten, to clear or release — the same French loan-family as English quit: a receipt quits your debt. [wiktionary]

firma.context_phrase: Er arbeitet bei einer großen Firma.
firma.context_translation: He works for a big company.
firma.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian firma, a signature from Latin firmare, to make firm — the page lists English firm as cognate. [wiktionary]

einkauf.context_translation: The shopping was a good deal today.
einkauf.etymology_derivation: ein + Kauf (buying): the in-buy; kaufen is the German twin of English cheap — both from Latin caupo, the tradesman (Old English ceapian, to trade). [wiktionary]

einkaufen.etymology_derivation: ein (in) + kaufen (to buy) — buy in, do the shopping; the kaufen root is the German twin of English cheap. [wiktionary]

kunde.context_phrase: Der Kunde wartet an der Kasse.
kunde.context_translation: The customer is waiting at the checkout.
kunde.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *kuntho, a known one — the page lists Old English cutha as cognate, the uncouth family: a customer is one you know. [wiktionary]

gitarre.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Spanish guitarra, from Arabic qithara, from Greek kithara - the same Spanish word that gave English guitar. [wiktionary]

radio.context_translation: We listen to the radio in the car.
radio.etymology_derivation: Borrowed about 1920 from English radio, short for radiotelegraphy - a straight English loan. [wiktionary]

computer.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English computer - a straight English loan. [wiktionary]

rad.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *raþą, from the PIE root *Hret- (to roll) - the same root that gave Latin rota and English rotary. [wiktionary]

reiten.context_translation: The child is learning to ride.
reiten.etymology_derivation: Class 1 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną - the exact twin of English ride: reiten-ritt-geritten matches ride-rode-ridden. [wiktionary]

segeln.context_phrase: Im Sommer segeln wir auf dem See.
segeln.context_translation: In summer we sail on the lake.
segeln.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *seglōn, the verb of Segel (sail) - the page lists English sail as a direct cognate. [wiktionary]

zeichnen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + K → CH
zeichnen.etymology_derivation: From Zeichen (sign, token) - compare English token: the same old word shifted by t-to-z and k-to-ch, like two-zwei and make-machen. [wiktionary]

fotografieren.context_translation: We are photographing the old houses.
fotografieren.etymology_derivation: A Greek-rooted international word in the -ieren loan-verb family; like all -ieren verbs its participle takes no ge-: fotografiert. [wiktionary]

angeln.context_translation: My grandpa is fishing at the lake.
angeln.etymology_derivation: To fish with an Angel (fishing rod, hook) - the same old word as English angle, which survives in angler. [wiktionary]

tauchen.context_translation: The diver dives in the sea.
tauchen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *dūkan (to dive) - the twin of English duck, shifted twice: d-to-t and k-to-ch, like day-Tag and make-machen. [wiktionary]

schach.etymology_derivation: From Arabic shah, from Persian shah (king) - the same word that gave English check and checkmate (Persian shah mat, the king is dead). [wiktionary][etymonline]

feiern.context_translation: We are celebrating a birthday today.
feiern.etymology_derivation: From Old High German firOn, from fira, from Latin feriae (festival days) - the same Latin word that became the English fair, a market held on feast days. [wiktionary][etymonline]

ausgehen.context_translation: Do you want to go out on Saturday?
ausgehen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *utgan (to go out), aus- + gehen - aus is the t-to-s twin of English out, as the old English cognate outgo shows. [wiktionary]

laufen.context_phrase: Ich laufe jeden Morgen im Park.
laufen.context_translation: I run every morning in the park.
laufen.etymology_derivation: Class 7 strong verb from Proto-West Germanic *hlaupan - the exact relative of English leap and lope; läuft-lief-gelaufen preserves the old ablaut. [wiktionary]

ski.etymology_derivation: A 19th-century borrowing of Norwegian ski, from Old Norse skíð (split stick) - English ski is the same Norwegian loan, and the native German doublet is Scheit (log). [wiktionary][etymonline]

deutsch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, of the people, built on *þeudō, people; the very same word as English Dutch, with Latin theodiscus and Teutonic sharing the root. [wiktionary]

französisch.etymology_derivation: From Old French francois plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; both trace back to the Franks, whence also English frank. [wiktionary]

englisch.etymology_derivation: From England plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the page itself names English English as the cognate, so this is the same word. [wiktionary]

spanisch.etymology_derivation: Spanien + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Spanish. [wiktionary]

italienisch.etymology_derivation: Italien + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Italian. [wiktionary]

türkisch.etymology_derivation: Türke + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Turkish. [wiktionary]

polnisch.etymology_derivation: Polen + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Polish. [wiktionary]

russisch.etymology_derivation: Russe + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the Rus name reached German via Medieval Latin Russus from Greek Rhos. [wiktionary]

chinesisch.etymology_derivation: From the noun Chinese plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish, which the page itself matches to English -ese. [wiktionary]

japanisch.etymology_derivation: Japan + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Japanese. [wiktionary]

amerikanisch.etymology_derivation: Amerika + the suffix -anisch, the twin of English -an in American; the same word as English American. [wiktionary]

sprache.context_phrase: Die Sprache ist schwer zu lernen.
sprache.context_translation: The language is hard to learn.
sprache.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sprāhha, Proto-West Germanic *sprāku, the twin of English speech; the k to ch velar shift links both to the sprechen and speak family. [wiktionary]

muttersprache.etymology_derivation: Mutter + Sprache, mother language; a loan translation of Latin lingua materna, the same mother-language metaphor as English mother tongue. [wiktionary]

hauptstadt.context_phrase: Berlin ist die Hauptstadt von Deutschland.
hauptstadt.context_translation: Berlin is the capital of Germany.
hauptstadt.etymology_derivation: Haupt + Stadt, literally head city; the page traces Haupt to the PIE head root that also yields Latin caput, so English capital is the Latin twin, and Stadt is the twin of English stead. [wiktionary]

staat.etymology_derivation: From Latin status via Old French estat, the same loan as English state; a doublet of German Status and Etat. [wiktionary]

summe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin summa, the total - English sum is the same Latin loan. [wiktionary]

rest.context_phrase: Der Rest des Kuchens ist für dich.
rest.context_translation: The rest of the cake is for you.
rest.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian resto, ultimately from Latin restare, to remain - English rest is a parallel loan from the same Latin verb. [wiktionary]

verwandte.etymology_derivation: Substantivized from the adjective verwandt, the past participle of verwenden; the etymology section on the page is empty, so the traditional link to English wend via wenden, to turn, is not documented there. [wiktionary] [UNVERIFIED - check]

enkelkind.context_translation: The grandchild is playing in the garden.
enkelkind.etymology_derivation: Enkel plus Kind; Enkel has no living English cognate, while Kind goes back to Proto-Indo-European genh1, the root of archaic English kin. [wiktionary]

priester.context_phrase: Der Priester wohnt neben der Kirche.
priester.context_translation: The priest lives next to the church.
priester.etymology_derivation: Both English priest and German Priester go back to Latin presbyter, from Greek presbyteros, elder - the same ecclesiastical loan, borrowed into German around the year 700. [wiktionary]

geschäftsmann.context_phrase: Der Geschäftsmann arbeitet in der Stadt.
geschäftsmann.context_translation: The businessman works in the city.
geschäftsmann.etymology_derivation: Compound of Geschäft (business) and Mann (man), the exact twin of English man; Geschäft is attested from Middle High German gescheft and Old High German giscaft, from the Germanic root family of schaffen and English shape [UNVERIFIED - check]. [wiktionary]

brezel.context_phrase: Die Brezel ist ein klassisches Gebäck aus München.
brezel.context_translation: The pretzel is a classic pastry from Munich.
brezel.etymology_derivation: From Vulgar Latin brachiātellus, a little cake shaped like bent arms, from Latin bracchium, arm; English borrowed pretzel directly from German Brezel. [wiktionary]

haselnuss.context_phrase: Ich mag Schokolade mit ganzen Haselnüssen.
haselnuss.context_translation: I like chocolate with whole hazelnuts.
haselnuss.etymology_derivation: Hasel + Nuss, the exact calque of hazelnut; the page names English hazelnut as a cognate, and Nuss is the documented twin of nut with t shifting to ss. [wiktionary]

walnuss.context_phrase: Die Walnüsse sind teuer im Winter.
walnuss.context_translation: The walnuts are expensive in winter.
walnuss.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic walhaz, foreign, plus hnuts, nut — the same foreign-nut compound as Old English wealhhnutu; the page names English walnut as a cognate. [wiktionary]

erdnuss.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
erdnuss.etymology_derivation: Erde + Nuss, literally earth-nut: Erde is the twin of earth (th to d) and Nuss the twin of nut (t to ss), the same building blocks as the English word earthnut. [wiktionary]

kokosnuss.context_translation: The coconut falls from the tree.
kokosnuss.etymology_derivation: Kokos + Nuss; the Nuss element is the documented twin of nut (t to ss), and Kokos is the same coco word that sits inside English coconut. [wiktionary]

vanille.context_translation: The ice cream tastes of vanilla.
vanille.etymology_derivation: Borrowed around 1700 from French vanille, from Spanish vainilla; English vanilla comes from the same Spanish word. [wiktionary]

zimt.context_phrase: Ich streue Zimt auf den Reis.
zimt.context_translation: I sprinkle cinnamon on the rice.
zimt.etymology_derivation: From Latin cinnamon, cinnamomum, through Greek kinnamomon, a Phoenician trade word per Herodotus; English cinnamon is a doublet of the same ancient spice word. [wiktionary]

nachtisch.etymology_derivation: nach + Tisch, with Tisch in its archaic sense meal; the documented twin of dish (Latin discus, d to t), so a Nachtisch is literally an after-dish. [wiktionary]

abendbrot.context_phrase: Um sechs essen wir das Abendbrot.
abendbrot.etymology_derivation: Abend + Brot, literally evening bread — the German supper; Abend is the twin of archaic English even and Brot the twin of bread. [wiktionary]

hobby.etymology_derivation: An unadapted borrowing of English hobby — the same word, kept with German spelling and plural Hobbys. [wiktionary]

freizeit.context_phrase: In meiner Freizeit lese ich Bücher.
freizeit.context_translation: In my free time I read books.
freizeit.etymology_derivation: frei + Zeit, literally free time; frei is the exact twin of free and Zeit the twin of time (as in tide, t to z). [wiktionary]

puppe.context_phrase: Das Kind spielt mit der Puppe.
puppe.context_translation: The child plays with the doll.
puppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin pupa, doll — the same Latin doll-word that gave English puppet through Old French popette. [wiktionary][etymonline]

würfel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wurpilaz, die, akin to *werpana, to throw — the same throw-family as English warp; the Germanic p surfaces as pf in German. [wiktionary]

grillen.context_phrase: Im Sommer grillen wir im Garten.
grillen.context_translation: In summer we grill in the garden.
grillen.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English grill — a modern loanword kept almost unchanged, with a Swiss synonym grillieren. [wiktionary]

stehlen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stelana, the same root as English steal; both keep the class-4 ablaut — steal, stole, stolen mirrors stehlen, stahl, gestohlen. [wiktionary]

diebstahl.context_phrase: Die Polizei meldet einen Diebstahl im Laden.
diebstahl.context_translation: The police report a theft in the shop.
diebstahl.etymology_derivation: Dieb + Stahl, a noun from stehlen: Dieb is the documented twin of thief (th to d, f to b) and stehlen the twin of steal — the German parallel to English theft. [wiktionary]

not.context_phrase: Er half mir in meiner Not.
not.context_translation: He helped me in my time of need.
not.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *naudi; the page lists English need as a direct cognate, with the d of need hardening to t in Not. [wiktionary]

patient.context_translation: The patient waits in the waiting room.
patient.etymology_derivation: From Latin patiens, the present participle of pati, to suffer — the same participle that gave English patient through Old French; a weak noun with plural Patienten. [wiktionary][etymonline]

klinik.etymology_derivation: A 19th-century learned word from Greek kline, bed (klinike techne, the bedside art) — the same Greek source as English clinic. [wiktionary]

operation.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin operatio, a performing, from operari (the root of operieren) — the same Latin word as English operation. [wiktionary]

operieren.context_phrase: Der Arzt operiert den Patienten heute.
operieren.context_translation: The doctor operates on the patient today.
operieren.etymology_derivation: From Latin operari, to work, plus the -ieren suffix — the standard Latin-loan verb pattern, exactly like operate; the participle is operiert with no ge- prefix. [wiktionary]

selbst.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *selbaz; the page lists English self as the direct cognate — the f closing to b in German plus an excrescent t. [wiktionary]

endlich.etymology_derivation: Ende + -lich, a formation the page itself compares to English endly; Ende is the documented twin of end. [wiktionary]

eben.context_translation: Just come along to the cinema.
eben.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *ebnaz, flat, even; the page lists English even as the direct cognate — the v closing to b in German. [wiktionary]

haushalt.etymology_derivation: Haus + halten, and the page lists English household as a cognate — the exact mirror, with halten the twin of hold (d to t). [wiktionary]

stockwerk.context_phrase: Die Küche ist im ersten Stockwerk.
stockwerk.context_translation: The kitchen is on the first floor.
stockwerk.etymology_derivation: Stock (stick, then storey) + Werk; Stock is the twin of stock and Werk the twin of work (k to ch) — a storey is literally a stock of the house. [wiktionary]

garderobe.context_phrase: Die Jacken hängen an der Garderobe.
garderobe.context_translation: The coats hang on the coat rack.
garderobe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French garde-robe, guard-robe — the exact compound of English wardrobe, whose warder is the same Frankish guard-word. [wiktionary][etymonline]

anker.context_phrase: Das Schiff setzt den Anker aus.
anker.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *ankurô, from Latin ancora, from Greek ankura — the same Greek-Latin borrowing as English anchor. [wiktionary]

landkarte.context_phrase: Wir suchen den Weg auf der Landkarte.
landkarte.context_translation: We look for the way on the map.
landkarte.etymology_derivation: Land + Karte, both documented twins: land, and Karte the twin of card (both from Latin charta) — a land-card, that is, a map. [wiktionary]

fahrgast.etymology_derivation: fahren + Gast, both documented twins (fare, guest) — the fare-guest, the one riding and paying. [wiktionary]

fußgänger.context_phrase: Der Fußgänger wartet an der Ampel.
fußgänger.context_translation: The pedestrian waits at the traffic light.
fußgänger.etymology_derivation: Fuß + Gänger, both documented twins (foot, and gehen the twin of go) — a foot-goer, what Latin-based English calls a pedestrian. [wiktionary]

brief.context_phrase: Ich schreibe einen Brief an Oma.
brief.context_translation: I am writing a letter to Grandma.
brief.etymology_derivation: From Latin breve, the neuter of brevis, short, first for a short papal document; the page lists English brief as a cognate borrowed from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

briefmarke.etymology_derivation: Brief (the twin of brief, both from Latin brevis, short) + Marke (the twin of mark, both from Germanic mark-, sign) — a letter-mark, that is, a postage stamp. [wiktionary]

postkarte.context_phrase: Wir schreiben eine Postkarte von Rom.
postkarte.context_translation: We are writing a postcard from Rome.
postkarte.etymology_derivation: Post + Karte, both documented twins (post, and Karte the twin of card) — a post-card, word for word. [wiktionary]

automat.context_phrase: Am Automat kaufe ich ein Ticket.
automat.context_translation: At the machine I buy a ticket.
automat.etymology_derivation: A learned borrowing from Latin automatum, from Greek automatos, self-acting — the same Greek word behind English automatic; American English automat came from German. [wiktionary]

gruppe.context_phrase: Unsere Gruppe trifft sich um acht.
gruppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French groupe, from Italian gruppo, ultimately from Germanic *kruppaz, lump — the same Romance round-trip word as English group. [wiktionary]

ausländer.etymology_derivation: Ausland + -er, from Middle High German uzlender; the page lists English outlander and outlandish as cognates — literally an out-lander. [wiktionary]

partner.context_phrase: Mein Partner und ich arbeiten zusammen.
partner.context_translation: My partner and I work together.
partner.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English partner — the same word, reshaped to German pronunciation, with feminine Partnerin. [wiktionary]

erwachsener.context_phrase: Nur Erwachsene zahlen den vollen Preis.
erwachsener.context_translation: Only adults pay the full price.
erwachsener.etymology_derivation: The nominalized adjective erwachsen, grown — the participle of wachsen, to grow, which the page lists as cognate with English wax, the old grow verb as in the waxing moon. [wiktionary]

fremder.context_phrase: Der Fremde fragt nach dem Weg.
fremder.context_translation: The stranger asks for the way.
fremder.etymology_derivation: fremd + -er; the dictionary documents fremd as the twin of the obsolete English word fremd, foreign — a stranger, a foreigner to you. [wiktionary]

vorfreude.context_phrase: Die Vorfreude auf den Urlaub ist groß.
vorfreude.context_translation: The anticipation of the holiday is great.
vorfreude.etymology_derivation: vor- + Freude, literally before-joy — the joy of looking forward; vor is the documented twin of fore, and Freude is the dictionary's joy-word. [wiktionary]

zweifel.context_phrase: Ich habe Zweifel an dem Plan.
zweifel.context_translation: I have doubts about the plan.
zweifel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *twifl, related to the root of zwei, two — being of two minds; English doubt did the same, from Latin dubitare, literally to be of two (duo). [wiktionary][etymonline]

humor.context_phrase: Er hat einen guten Sinn für Humor.
humor.context_translation: He has a good sense of humor.
humor.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin humor; the modern funny sense was a semantic loan from English humour — the same word, with English even lending it its meaning. [wiktionary]

kreuzung.etymology_derivation: kreuzen + -ung, from Kreuz, borrowed from Latin crux, crucis — the same Latin word that gave English cross, which English took via Old Irish and Old Norse. [wiktionary][etymonline]

platz.context_phrase: Der Platz vor dem Rathaus ist alt.
platz.context_translation: The square in front of the town hall is old.
platz.etymology_derivation: From Old French place, from Latin platea, from Greek plateia, broad way; the page names English place as a cognate — the same Latin-Greek square-word. [wiktionary]

umweg.context_phrase: Wir nehmen einen Umweg wegen der Baustelle.
umweg.context_translation: We take a detour because of the construction site.
umweg.etymology_derivation: um + Weg, from Middle High German umbe, around, plus wec, way; Weg is the documented twin of way — an around-way, a detour. [wiktionary]

quer.context_phrase: Der Baum liegt quer über dem Weg.
quer.context_translation: The tree lies across the path.
quer.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *þwerh, oblique (Old High German twerh); etymonline lists German quer as a cognate of English thwart, from Old Norse þverr, across. [wiktionary][etymonline]

weste.context_phrase: Im Winter trage ich eine Weste.
weste.context_translation: In winter I wear a vest.
weste.etymology_derivation: From French veste (17th century), from Latin vestis, garment — the same French word that gave English vest. [wiktionary]

sonnenbrille.context_phrase: Im Sommer brauche ich die Sonnenbrille.
sonnenbrille.context_translation: In summer I need the sunglasses.
sonnenbrille.etymology_derivation: Sonne + -n- + Brille, the exact mirror of sunglasses: Sonne is the documented twin of sun, and Brille is the dictionary's glasses-word. [wiktionary]

stehen.context_phrase: Ich stehe am Fenster und sehe hinaus.
stehen.context_translation: I stand at the window and look out.
stehen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stāną; the page documents cognate English stand, the same stand-verb family (English stood, German stand). [wiktionary]

setzen.context_phrase: Ich setze mich auf den Stuhl.
setzen.context_translation: I sit down on the chair.
setzen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *sattjan, a causative of sit; the page documents cognate English set. The t of set reappears as z (ts) in setzen, the same sibilant shift as two and zwei. [wiktionary]

zeigen.context_phrase: Kannst du mir den Weg zeigen?
zeigen.context_translation: Can you show me the way?
zeigen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German zeigōn, an intensive of zīhan; the page traces it to PIE *deyḱ- and notes that the root also gave Zeichen and English teach. The t of teach corresponds to the z of zeigen. [wiktionary]

schauen.context_phrase: Wir schauen das Spiel im Fernsehen.
schauen.context_translation: We watch the game on TV.
schauen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (to look); the page cites Old English scēawian and compares English show — the old look-verb that English turned into show. [wiktionary]

fallen.context_phrase: Das Glas ist vom Tisch gefallen.
fallen.context_translation: The glass fell off the table.
fallen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fallaną; the page lists English fall among the akin forms — a class 7 strong verb on both sides: fell and fiel, fallen and gefallen. [wiktionary]

beginnen.context_phrase: Der Film beginnt um acht Uhr.
beginnen.context_translation: The film begins at eight o'clock.
beginnen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *biginnaną; the page documents cognate English begin — an exact class 3 ablaut twin: began and begann, begun and begonnen. [wiktionary]

kennen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *kannijaną, a causative of *kunnaną (can); the page lists English ken (as in beyond my ken) — the same knowing-verb English keeps in Scotland. [wiktionary]

fangen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fanhaną; the page lists English fang (to lay hold of) — the old catch-verb that survives in English as the tooth that catches. [wiktionary]

hängen.context_phrase: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
hängen.context_translation: The picture hangs on the wall.
hängen.etymology_derivation: A merger of three old hang-verbs, back to Proto-Germanic *hanhaną and *hangijaną; the page documents cognate English hang — strong like hang-hung (hing, gehangen). [wiktionary]

blasen.context_translation: The wind is blowing hard today.
blasen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *blāsan, a class 7 strong verb (blies, geblasen); the fetched page gives no English cognate, but the standard twin is English blow (blew, blown). [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

rennen.context_phrase: Die Kinder rennen durch den Park.
rennen.context_translation: The children run through the park.
rennen.etymology_derivation: A merger of the causative *rannijaną and the intransitive *rinnaną (to run); the page notes the same root merger happened in English run. [wiktionary]

lügen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *leuganą; the page documents cognate English lie (the tell-a-lie one). The ü spelling was standardized to keep the word apart from liegen (to lie down). [wiktionary]

merken.context_translation: I make a note of your number.
merken.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *markijaną (to mark, notice) — the mark- root behind English mark and remark. [wiktionary]

tat.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *dādi; the page compares English deed — the same do-word with the d to t hardening, as in day and Tag. [wiktionary]

holen.context_phrase: Ich hole Wasser aus der Küche.
holen.context_translation: I am getting water from the kitchen.
holen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *holōną (to fetch); the page documents cognate English haul — the same hauling-and-fetching word. [wiktionary]

lehren.etymology_derivation: The causative of the lore root (*laizō): German splits the learn family into lernen (learn) and lehren (teach); the page documents archaic English lear as cognate and glosses the root noun as lore. [wiktionary]

winken.etymology_derivation: From the *wink- root (to sway, wink); the page lists English wink as cognate — in German it means waving hello and goodbye. [wiktionary]

buchstabe.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *bōkstabô, literally book-stave: each letter was a stave carved for writing, first on beechwood; the page compares English bookstaff and bookstave. [wiktionary]

halten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *haldaną — English hold is the documented cognate; German hardened d to t (the stop shift). Strong verb, class 7: hielt, gehalten. [wiktionary]

lassen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *lētaną via Proto-West Germanic *lātan — English let is the documented cognate; the old t survives in English but hissed to ss in German. Strong verb: ließ, gelassen. [wiktionary]

treten.context_translation: Do not step in the puddle.
treten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *trudaną — English tread is the documented cognate; the same class 5 ablaut: tritt, trat ↔ tread, trod. [wiktionary]

fliegen.context_translation: We are flying to Rome tomorrow.
fliegen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (PIE *plewk-) — English fly is the documented cognate; strong verb: flog, geflogen. [wiktionary]

gewinnen.context_phrase: Unser Team will das Spiel gewinnen.
gewinnen.context_translation: Our team wants to win the game.
gewinnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *winnaną (PIE *wenh₁-) — English win descends from the same root (Old English winnan); strong verb: gewann, gewonnen. [wiktionary]

schlagen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *slahaną — English slay (Old English slēan) and slog are documented cognates; strong verb: schlug, geschlagen. [wiktionary]

schießen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skeutaną — English shoot is the documented cognate (Old English scēotan); strong verb: schoss, geschossen. [wiktionary]

springen.context_phrase: Das Kind springt über den Bach.
springen.context_translation: The child jumps over the brook.
springen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *springaną (PIE *sprenǵʰ-) — English spring is the documented cognate; strong verb: sprang, gesprungen. [wiktionary]

bitten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *bidjaną — English bid is the documented cognate (Old English biddan); strong verb: bat, gebeten. [wiktionary]

fliehen.context_phrase: Die Familie flieht vor dem Feuer.
fliehen.context_translation: The family flees from the fire.
fliehen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fleuhaną — English flee is the documented cognate (Old English flēon); German kept the old strong past floh, geflohen. [wiktionary]

küssen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kussijan — English kiss is the documented cognate; a doubled expressive kk that both languages kept. [wiktionary]

grüßen.context_phrase: Ich grüße meine Nachbarin jeden Morgen.
grüßen.context_translation: I greet my neighbor every morning.
grüßen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *grōtijan — English greet is the documented cognate; the old t hissed to ß in German (the sibilant shift). [wiktionary]

reichen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *raikijaną — English reach is the documented cognate; the old k softened to ch (the velar shift). [wiktionary]

heben.context_translation: Do not lift such heavy boxes.
heben.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *habbjan — English heave is the documented cognate (Dutch heffen); strong verb: hob, gehoben. [wiktionary]

schieben.context_phrase: Wir schieben den Wagen von Hand.
schieben.context_translation: We push the car by hand.
schieben.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skeubaną (PIE *skewbʰ-) — English shove is the documented cognate; strong verb: schob, geschoben. [wiktionary]

raten.context_phrase: Ich rate dir zu einer Pause.
raten.context_translation: I advise you to take a break.
raten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *rēdaną — English read and archaic rede are documented cognates; German kept the advising sense and hardened d to t. [wiktionary]

füttern.context_phrase: Wir füttern die Enten im Park.
füttern.context_translation: We feed the ducks in the park.
füttern.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (Futter + -n) — dialectal English to fodder is the documented cognate. [wiktionary]

richten.context_phrase: Richte die Bilder an der Wand.
richten.context_translation: Straighten the pictures on the wall.
richten.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *rihtijan (to right) — English right is the documented cognate; the gh that went silent in English still sounds as ch in German. [wiktionary]

fall.context_phrase: In diesem Fall nehme ich den Bus.
fall.context_translation: In this case I take the bus.
fall.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fall — English fall is the documented cognate; the grammar sense (in diesem Fall) is a calque of Latin casus. [wiktionary]

ab.context_phrase: Ab morgen bin ich im Urlaub.
ab.context_translation: From tomorrow I am on vacation.
ab.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ab — English off and of are cognates at the Proto-Indo-European level (*h₂epó); the entry compares German ab, Dutch af, English off. [wiktionary]

gesundheit.context_translation: Health is more important than money.
gesundheit.etymology_derivation: Gesund (healthy) plus -heit (-ness); the page documents gesund as cognate with English sound — the old healthy-word alive in English in of sound mind. [wiktionary]

kauen.context_phrase: Kau dein Essen langsam und gut.
kauen.context_translation: Chew your food slowly and well.
kauen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *keuwan, PIE *ǵyewh₁-; the page lists English chew as cognate — English palatalized the old k to ch, German kept it as k. [wiktionary]

stinken.context_translation: The garbage can stinks in summer.
stinken.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną; the page says compare English stink — the same smell-word with the same ablaut: stink-stank-stunk, stinken-stank-gestunken. [wiktionary]

pflaster.context_phrase: Ich klebe ein Pflaster auf die Wunde.
pflaster.context_translation: I stick a plaster on the wound.
pflaster.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin plastrum via Proto-West Germanic *plastr and Old High German pflastar — the p became pf in German, while English plaster kept p, borrowed from the same Latin source. [wiktionary]

wunde.context_phrase: Die Wunde am Bein heilt gut.
wunde.context_translation: The wound on the leg is healing well.
wunde.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wundō, from *wundaz, wounded; the page lists English wound as cognate — the same wound-word carried sound-alike into both languages. [wiktionary]

anders.context_translation: In Germany many things are different.
anders.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *anþeraz (documented on the page); the High German d is the shifted th of English other, the same dental hardening as think and denken. [wiktionary]

fest.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fastuz (firm); the same word as English fast, which kept the old firm sense in hold fast and stuck fast before it came to mean quick. [wiktionary]

gemein.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *gamainī (shared, common); the page documents cognate English mean — both words slid from common to lowly to nasty. [wiktionary]

fett.context_phrase: Diese Wurst ist zu fett für mich.
fett.context_translation: This sausage is too fatty for me.
fett.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *faitid; the page compares English fat — the same Germanic fat-word (German doublet: feist). [wiktionary]

übel.context_translation: I feel a bit sick today.
übel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *ubil — English evil is the documented cognate; both descend from the same ancient word for bad. [wiktionary]

zäh.context_translation: The old chewing gum is tough.
zäh.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *tą̄h(ī) — English tough is the documented cognate; English kept the t and spelled the gh, German shifted t to z and lost the h. Doublet of German taff. [wiktionary]

nadel.context_phrase: Ich nähe mit Nadel und Faden.
nadel.context_translation: I sew with needle and thread.
nadel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *nāþlu, from the sew-root (PIE *(s)neh₁-); the page documents cognate English needle — the same sewing-word. [wiktionary]

handtasche.etymology_derivation: Hand + Tasche — the exact compound calque of handbag; both elements are documented twins. [wiktionary]

regenmantel.etymology_derivation: Regen + Mantel — the compound calque of raincoat; Regen is the twin of rain (y → g). [wiktionary]

theater.context_translation: We are going to the theater today.
theater.etymology_derivation: From French théâtre, from Latin theātrum, from Greek theātron (a place for viewing) — the same viewing-place word English took as theater. [wiktionary]

schwimmbad.context_phrase: Das Schwimmbad ist im Sommer voll.
schwimmbad.context_translation: The swimming pool is full in summer.
schwimmbad.etymology_derivation: schwimmen + Bad — the swim-bath; both elements are documented twins (swim, bath). [wiktionary]

fernsehen.etymology_derivation: fern + sehen — literally far-seeing; the entry calls it a calque of French télévision, the same idea as English television. [wiktionary]

handschrift.etymology_derivation: Hand + Schrift — handwriting; Schrift is the noun of schreiben (the scribe family). [wiktionary]

fußballspieler.etymology_derivation: Fußball + Spieler — part-for-part football player; Fußball itself is the foot-ball calque and Spieler the player of Spiel. [wiktionary]

sportplatz.context_phrase: Die Kinder spielen auf dem Sportplatz.
sportplatz.context_translation: The children play on the sports field.
sportplatz.etymology_derivation: Sport + Platz — the sports field; both elements are shared loans (Sport, Platz/place). [wiktionary]

raum.context_phrase: Der Raum ist groß und hell.
raum.context_translation: The room is large and bright.
raum.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *rūmą (space); the same word as English room — German diphthongized the long u to au. [wiktionary]

toilette.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French toilette around 1700 — the very same French word that English took as toilet. [wiktionary]

dusche.context_translation: I will take a quick shower.
dusche.etymology_derivation: Borrowed via French douche from Italian doccia — the same French word English took as douche; German replaced the older Brausebad over its bad connotations. [wiktionary]

wohnung.context_phrase: Meine Wohnung ist im dritten Stock.
wohnung.context_translation: My apartment is on the third floor.
wohnung.etymology_derivation: Wohnen (to dwell) plus -ung; the page documents the archaic English cognate woning (dwelling-place) from the same dwelling-word. [wiktionary]

hochhaus.context_phrase: Wir wohnen in einem alten Hochhaus.
hochhaus.context_translation: We live in an old high-rise.
hochhaus.etymology_derivation: hoch + Haus — the high house, what English calls a high-rise; hoch is the twin of high (gh → ch). [wiktionary]

niederlande.context_phrase: Wir fahren mit dem Auto in die Niederlande.
niederlande.context_translation: We drive to the Netherlands by car.
niederlande.etymology_derivation: nieder (low) plus Lande — the exact counterpart of English Netherlands; the page glosses nieder as nether, its th to d twin (as in denken and think). [wiktionary]

freundschaft.context_phrase: Unsere Freundschaft ist zehn Jahre alt.
freundschaft.context_translation: Our friendship is ten years old.
freundschaft.etymology_derivation: Freund (friend) plus -schaft, the exact twin of English -ship; Proto-West Germanic *friundskapi is friendship part for part. [wiktionary]

essig.context_phrase: Ich mag Salat mit Öl und Essig.
essig.context_translation: I like salad with oil and vinegar.
essig.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *atek, a metathesized variant of *aket (vinegar), from Latin acētum; the same sharp-sour root (PIE *h₂eḱ-) that gives the sour part of English vinegar (sour wine). [wiktionary]

butterbrot.context_phrase: Ich nehme ein Butterbrot mit in die Schule.
butterbrot.context_translation: I take a sandwich to school.
butterbrot.etymology_derivation: Butter + Brot — both elements are documented twins (Butter via Latin butyrum, Brot kin to brew); an exact internal calque. [wiktionary]

wachsen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *wahsan, a class 6 strong verb (wuchs, gewachsen); the page documents cognate English wax in its older become sense — the moon still waxes. [wiktionary]

wasserfall.context_phrase: Der Wasserfall fällt in den tiefen See.
wasserfall.context_translation: The waterfall falls into the deep lake.
wasserfall.etymology_derivation: Wasser + Fall — the exact compound calque of waterfall; Wasser carries the sibilant shift (t → ss), Fall is the twin of fall. [wiktionary]

klassenzimmer.etymology_derivation: Klasse + Zimmer — the classroom; Klasse is the same Latin loan as English class, Zimmer originally timber-work, kin to English timber. IPA derived from the verified components (page has none). [wiktionary]

handwerk.context_translation: My uncle is learning a trade.
handwerk.etymology_derivation: Hand + Werk — Proto-Germanic *handuwerką; the entry points to English handiwork, and Werk carries the PIE *werǵ- root of work. [wiktionary]

sparen.context_phrase: Ich spare Geld für den Urlaub.
sparen.context_translation: I am saving money for the vacation.
sparen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *sparēn; the page compares English spare — the same saving-word. [wiktionary]

steuer.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German stiure (support); the page traces the sense from helm to supporting post to support money to tax and documents cognate English steer — what you pay keeps the ship of state on course. [wiktionary][dwds]

rabatt.context_phrase: Heute gibt es zwanzig Prozent Rabatt.
rabatt.context_translation: Today there is twenty percent off.
rabatt.etymology_derivation: From Italian rabbatto via French rabat, from Latin battuere (to beat down); the page documents cognate English rebate — a price beaten down. [wiktionary]

gefahr.context_translation: Be careful, there is danger here.
gefahr.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fērō (danger); the page documents cognate English fear — fear began as the danger itself. [wiktionary]

polizei.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Medieval Latin policia, from Late Latin polītīa — the same city-word (Greek polis) behind English police. [wiktionary]

feuerwehr.context_translation: The fire brigade puts out the fire.
feuerwehr.etymology_derivation: Feuer (fire, a documented twin) plus Wehr (defense) from the ward-off root *warjaną; the related Wehr entry names English weir — a river weir is a Wehr in the water. [wiktionary]

unterschrift.context_phrase: Ich brauche deine Unterschrift auf dem Formular.
unterschrift.context_translation: I need your signature on the form.
unterschrift.etymology_derivation: unter + Schrift (from unterschreiben) — literally underwrit, the Germanic calque of Latin subscriptio; schreiben is the Latin-loan twin of scribe. [wiktionary]

ostern.context_translation: We look for Easter eggs at Easter.
ostern.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ōstarūn, from Proto-West Germanic *Austrā; the page compares English Easter — the same Germanic festival name of the dawn-east direction (cf. Osten, east). [wiktionary]

mal.context_phrase: Komm ein Mal mit ins Kino.
mal.context_translation: Come along to the cinema one time.
mal.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mēlą — English meal is the documented cognate (Mahl is the same word); ein Mal counts the times, as in piecemeal. [wiktionary]

wochentag.context_phrase: Am Wochentag arbeite ich bis fünf.
wochentag.context_translation: On a weekday I work until five.
wochentag.etymology_derivation: Woche + Tag — the exact compound of weekday; both elements are documented twins (week, day). [wiktionary]

buchen.context_translation: I am booking a hotel online.
buchen.etymology_derivation: From Buch plus -en (the beechwood-carving word); the modern reserve sense was modelled after English to book — a semantic loan the page documents. [wiktionary]

schild.context_phrase: Das Schild zeigt den Weg zum Bahnhof.
schild.context_translation: The sign shows the way to the station.
schild.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skelduz; the page documents cognate English shield — das Schild is the street sign, der Schild the shield. [wiktionary]

stau.context_translation: There is a traffic jam on the motorway.
stau.etymology_derivation: From Low German stouwe (weir), a back-formation of stauen (to dam up); the page compares English stow — traffic stowed on the motorway. [wiktionary]

flug.context_phrase: Unser Flug geht um sieben Uhr.
flug.context_translation: Our flight leaves at seven o'clock.
flug.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *flugiz, the noun of the fly-verb family (fliegen, to fly); the same flug- stem that gives English flight. [wiktionary]

hauptbahnhof.context_translation: We are meeting at the main station.
hauptbahnhof.etymology_derivation: Haupt + Bahnhof — the head-station; Haupt traces to the Proto-Indo-European *kap- head root (Latin caput, English head). [wiktionary]

großstadt.context_phrase: Die Großstadt ist laut, aber spannend.
großstadt.context_translation: The big city is loud but exciting.
großstadt.etymology_derivation: groß + Stadt — the big city; groß is the twin of great (t → ß). [wiktionary]

schneemann.context_translation: The children are building a snowman.
schneemann.etymology_derivation: Schnee + Mann — the exact compound calque of snowman; both elements are documented twins. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.

compounds.lore: Parts: kühl (cool) + Schrank (cabinet / cupboard) A cabinet designed to keep things cool. German describes the exact engineering function. The "oo" to "ü" vowel shift connects "cool" and "kühl".
compounds.example_sentence: Die Milch steht im Kühlschrank.
compounds.example_translation: The milk is in the fridge.

compounds.lore: Parts: Hand (hand) + Schuh (shoe) Why invent a new word when you can just call it a "shoe for your hand"? In German, a thimble is a "Fingerhut" (finger-hat) and a glove is a "Handschuh" (hand-shoe)!
compounds.example_sentence: Im Winter trage ich warme Handschuhe.
compounds.example_translation: In winter I wear warm gloves.

compounds.real_meaning: weight gain from comfort eating during emotional stress
compounds.lore: Parts: Kummer (grief / sorrow / worry) + Speck (bacon / pork fat) The physical accumulation of "bacon" you put on when comforting sorrow with comfort food! A uniquely vivid German cultural term with no single-word English equivalent.
compounds.example_sentence: Nach der Trennung hat sie viel Kummerspeck angesetzt.
compounds.example_translation: After the breakup she put on a lot of comfort-eating weight.

compounds.real_meaning: a stinging slap across the face
compounds.lore: Parts: Backe (cheek (of face)) + Pfeife (whistle / pipe (p → pf)) A slap delivered with such force that it makes the cheek "whistle" with a ringing sound! Leads to the famous compound "Backpfeifengesicht" — a face that looks like it urgently needs to be slapped.
compounds.example_sentence: Für den Witz hat er eine Backpfeife bekommen.
compounds.example_translation: He got a slap in the face for that joke.

compounds.lore: Parts: gegen (against / opposite (cf. again)) + Stand (standing / posture) A direct medieval calque of Latin "ob-jectum" (ob = against/gegen + jacere/jectum = thrown/standing). German scholars translated abstract Latin philosophy into tangible Germanic physical roots.
compounds.example_sentence: Was ist das für ein Gegenstand auf dem Tisch?
compounds.example_translation: What kind of object is that on the table?

compounds.lore: Parts: be- (prefix forming transitives) + Griff (grip / grasp (p → f)) A direct loan-translation of Latin "conceptus" (from con- + capere, to grasp/seize together). To understand something mentally is literally to "grasp" it (begreifen).
compounds.example_sentence: Dieser Begriff ist schwer zu erklären.
compounds.example_translation: This term is hard to explain.

compounds.lore: Parts: wahr (true / real (cognate with very/veracity)) + Nehmung (taking (from nehmen)) A philosophical calque of Latin "per-ceptio" — literally "taking something to be true". To perceive is "wahrnehmen" (to take as true).
compounds.example_sentence: Seine Wahrnehmung der Welt ist sehr scharf.
compounds.example_translation: His perception of the world is very sharp.

compounds.lore: Parts: Leid (suffering / sorrow / loath) + -schaft (-ship / condition (suffix)) A 17th-century calque of Latin "passio" (from pati = to suffer). True passion involves suffering for what you love! Coined in 1640 by German grammarian Christian Gueintz.
compounds.example_sentence: Sie spielt Klavier mit großer Leidenschaft.
compounds.example_translation: She plays piano with great passion.

compounds.lore: Parts: Wasser (water (t → ss)) + Stoff (matter / stuff / element) Direct calque of Greek "hydro-gen" (water-maker). German straightforwardly called it "water-stuff"! Oxygen is similarly "Sauerstoff" (sour-stuff, from Greek oxy-gen) and Nitrogen is "Stickstoff" (suffocate-stuff).
compounds.example_sentence: Wasser besteht aus Wasserstoff und Sauerstoff.
compounds.example_translation: Water consists of hydrogen and oxygen.

compounds.lore: Parts: krank (sick / ill) + Haus (house) No Latin obfuscation: it is simply the house for the sick. A nurse is a "Krankenschwester" (sick-sister) or "Krankenpfleger" (sick-carer).
compounds.example_sentence: Mein Onkel liegt im Krankenhaus.
compounds.example_translation: My uncle is in the hospital.

compounds.lore: Parts: krank (sick / ill) + Schwester (sister (cognate)) Historical origin from religious nursing orders where caregivers were addressed as "sister". Male nurses are traditionally "Krankenpfleger" (sick-carer).
compounds.example_sentence: Die Krankenschwester misst mein Fieber.
compounds.example_translation: The nurse takes my temperature.

compounds.lore: Parts: Staub (dust) + Sauger (sucker / suction device) A machine that literally sucks dust. Straight to the point. German nouns ending in "-er" derived from verbs (saugen → Sauger) are always masculine (der).
compounds.example_sentence: Der Staubsauger ist sehr laut.
compounds.example_translation: The vacuum cleaner is very loud.

compounds.lore: Parts: Flug (flight) + Zeug (stuff / apparatus / gear) The word "-zeug" means "stuff". An airplane is "flight-stuff", a lighter is "Feuerzeug" (fire-stuff), and a vehicle is "Fahrzeug" (drive-stuff)! Toys are "Spielzeug" (play-stuff) and tools are "Werkzeug" (work-stuff).
compounds.example_sentence: Das Flugzeug landet um acht Uhr.
compounds.example_translation: The plane lands at eight o'clock.

compounds.lore: Parts: Feuer (fire) + Zeug (stuff / apparatus) Apparatus designed to produce fire. Compound with "-zeug" is always neuter (das).
compounds.example_sentence: Hast du ein Feuerzeug?
compounds.example_translation: Do you have a lighter?

compounds.lore: Parts: fahren (to drive / fare) + Zeug (stuff / apparatus) Any apparatus used for faring or journeying on wheels. Compare with "Schlagzeug" (hit-stuff = drum set)!
compounds.example_sentence: Das Fahrzeug steht vor dem Haus.
compounds.example_translation: The vehicle is parked in front of the house.

compounds.lore: Parts: schlagen (to strike / hit (slay)) + Zeug (gear / apparatus) A collection of instruments whose entire purpose is to be hit with sticks. A stroke or heartbeat is a "Herzschlag" (heart-strike).
compounds.example_sentence: Mein Bruder spielt Schlagzeug in einer Band.
compounds.example_translation: My brother plays drums in a band.

compounds.lore: Parts: spielen (to play) + Zeug (stuff / gear) Any gear designed for playing games. A video game is a "Computerspiel".
compounds.example_sentence: Das Kind räumt sein Spielzeug auf.
compounds.example_translation: The child tidies up his toys.

compounds.real_meaning: corner store open late at night
compounds.lore: Parts: spät (late) + Kauf (purchase / buy) The famous Berlin "Späti" is shorthand for Spätkauf — literally where you buy things late. English "cheap" and German "kaufen" share Proto-Germanic *kaup- (trade/market).
compounds.example_sentence: Nach zehn Uhr kaufe ich Wasser im Spätkauf.
compounds.example_translation: After ten o'clock I buy water at the late-night shop.

compounds.lore: Parts: fern (far / distant) + Seher (seer / viewer) An exact morphological mirror of Greek tele (far) + Latin vision (seeing). German used its native Germanic roots! A telescope is similarly a "Fernrohr" (far-tube).
compounds.example_sentence: Der Fernseher läuft den ganzen Tag.
compounds.example_translation: The TV is on all day.

compounds.lore: Parts: auf (up / upon) + Zug (pull / train / draught) A contraption that pulls you upwards. A train is "der Zug" (the puller), an elevator is "der Aufzug" (the up-puller), and a parade is "der Umzug" (the around-pull).
compounds.example_sentence: Der Aufzug ist leider kaputt.
compounds.example_translation: Unfortunately the elevator is broken.

compounds.lore: Parts: Apfel (apple) + Kuchen (cake) Both components are English cognates shifted: Apple (p→pf) + Cake (k→ch)! Compound nouns in German always take the gender and plural form of the LAST word: der Kuchen → der Apfelkuchen.
compounds.example_sentence: Meine Oma backt den besten Apfelkuchen.
compounds.example_translation: My grandma bakes the best apple cake.

compounds.lore: Parts: Kinder (children) + Garten (garden) Coined by German educator Friedrich Fröbel in 1840 to symbolize children growing naturally like plants. Borrowed directly into English without translation.
compounds.example_sentence: Unsere Tochter geht schon in den Kindergarten.
compounds.example_translation: Our daughter already goes to kindergarten.

compounds.lore: Parts: glühen (to glow (cognate with glow)) + Birne (pear (fruit)) Germans saw the glass bulb shape and named it a "glowing pear"! German describes shapes by comparing them to common orchard fruits.
compounds.example_sentence: Die Glühbirne im Flur ist durchgebrannt.
compounds.example_translation: The light bulb in the hallway has burned out.

compounds.lore: Parts: Finger (finger) + Hut (hat / cap (hood)) A protective metal cap is simply a little hat for your finger. Foxglove flowers are also called "Fingerhut" in German because the blossoms look like tiny thimbles!
compounds.example_sentence: Beim Nähen trägt sie einen Fingerhut.
compounds.example_translation: When sewing she wears a thimble.

compounds.lore: Parts: Zahn (tooth (t → z)) + Arzt (doctor / physician) Direct and transparent: the doctor who fixes teeth. An eye doctor is an "Augenarzt" (eye-doctor), a vet is a "Tierarzt" (animal-doctor).
compounds.example_sentence: Morgen habe ich einen Termin beim Zahnarzt.
compounds.example_translation: Tomorrow I have an appointment at the dentist.

compounds.lore: Parts: Eisen (iron (cognate with iron)) + Bahn (track / path / way) The track made of iron. Parallels French "chemin de fer" (iron road).
compounds.example_sentence: Die Eisenbahn verbindet die beiden Städte.
compounds.example_translation: The railway connects the two cities.

compounds.lore: Parts: Auto (automobile) + Bahn (track / way) The dedicated track for cars. The German Autobahn is famous worldwide for having sections without advisory speed limits.
compounds.example_sentence: Auf der Autobahn gibt es oft Stau.
compounds.example_translation: There is often a traffic jam on the highway.

compounds.lore: Parts: Donner (thunder (th → d)) + Tag (day (d → t & y → g)) Day of the Norse thunder god Thor. Days of the week in German are always masculine (der).
compounds.example_sentence: Am Donnerstag gehen wir ins Kino.
compounds.example_translation: On Thursday we are going to the cinema.

compounds.lore: Parts: Mitte (middle / mid) + Woche (week (k → ch)) Replaced pagan Woden's day with geographical mid-week. The only German weekday name that doesn't end in "-tag".
compounds.example_sentence: Der Kurs findet jeden Mittwoch statt.
compounds.example_translation: The course takes place every Wednesday.

compounds.lore: Parts: über (over / beyond) + morgen (tomorrow) English used to have the word "overmorrow" (an exact twin), but abandoned it. German kept it! Similarly, "vorgestern" means "before-yesterday" (the day before yesterday).
compounds.example_sentence: Übermorgen fahre ich nach Berlin.
compounds.example_translation: The day after tomorrow I am going to Berlin.

compounds.lore: Parts: vor (before / fore-) + gestern (yesterday (y → g)) Symmetrical twin to übermorgen. Yester- in English is the same root as German gestern.
compounds.example_sentence: Vorgestern habe ich meine Tante besucht.
compounds.example_translation: The day before yesterday I visited my aunt.

compounds.lore: Parts: nach / nah (near / toward) + Bauer / bar (dweller / builder) Old English neahgebur (nigh + boor) is the exact same structure as German Nach-bar. The silent "gh" in English neighbor preserves the German "ch" [x] in Nachbar.
compounds.example_sentence: Unser Nachbar grüßt immer freundlich.
compounds.example_translation: Our neighbor always greets us in a friendly way.

falseFriends.trap_note: In German, a "Gift" can kill you. (For a present, use "das Geschenk").
You "bekommen" a package from the postman, not a butterfly! (For "to become", use "werden").
falseFriends.example_sentence: Ich habe heute ein Paket bekommen.

falseFriends.trap_note: Your "Chef" is the person signing your paycheck, not necessarily someone holding a spatula! (For kitchen cook, use "der Koch").
falseFriends.example_sentence: Mein Chef ist heute nicht im Büro.
falseFriends.example_translation: My boss is not in the office today.

falseFriends.trap_note: Your "Handy" is the phone in your hand. A pseudo-Anglicism coined in Germany in the 1990s!
falseFriends.example_sentence: Mein Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.
falseFriends.example_translation: My mobile phone is on the table.

falseFriends.trap_note: Die "aktuelle Nachricht" is the latest breaking news, not the "actual" truth! (For actual, use "tatsächlich" or "wirklich").
falseFriends.example_sentence: Hier finde ich die aktuellen Nachrichten.
falseFriends.example_translation: Here I find the current news.

falseFriends.trap_note: Asking someone for "Rat" means asking for advice, not a rodent! (For rat, use "die Ratte").
Ein "braves Kind" is a well-behaved good child, not a fearless warrior!
falseFriends.example_sentence: Sei brav und hör auf deine Mutter.
falseFriends.example_translation: Be good and listen to your mother.

falseFriends.trap_note: A "Fabrik" is the factory building where things are fabricated! (For cloth, use "der Stoff").
You study calculus and literature at a "Gymnasium", you do not do bench presses!
falseFriends.example_translation: My son goes to the Gymnasium (academic high school).

falseFriends.trap_note: In "Rente" gehen means to retire on a pension! (For apartment rent, use "die Miete").
falseFriends.example_sentence: Mein Opa bekommt jeden Monat seine Rente.
falseFriends.example_translation: My grandpa gets his pension every month.

falseFriends.trap_note: Der Kölner Dom is the massive Cologne Cathedral, regardless of whether it has a curved dome!
